# DataFn Documentation (Full)

> Self-hosted data sync SDK with offline-first storage, reactive signals, capability-driven schemas, and a structured query language (DFQL). Works with TypeScript, Python, and Swift.

This document contains the full content of the DataFn documentation, optimized for LLM consumption.


================================================================================
## Ai Resources
================================================================================


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Claude

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/ai-resources/claude
Description: Wire DataFn into Claude Code and Claude Desktop with project memory, raw-markdown lookups, and MCP.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Claude Code

Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` from the project root on every session start. This file is the primary surface for teaching Claude about your DataFn conventions.

### CLAUDE.md starter

```md
# Project: <name>

This project uses DataFn as the data layer.

## Architecture
- Server: TypeScript, mounted on Hono via `@datafn/http-hono`.
- Database: Postgres via Drizzle.
- Client: React + `@datafn/client`.
- Auth: AuthFn provides sessions; the namespaceProvider derives `ns(orgId, userId)`.

## DataFn conventions
- Schemas live in `shared/schema.ts` and are imported by both server and client.
- All resource access goes through DFQL. We do not query the database directly outside of migrations.
- Mutations are wrapped in transactions when more than one record changes.
- Field-level authorization rules live in `server/authz.ts`.
- Error envelopes are surfaced to the UI via the `useError` hook.

## When implementing a feature
1. Add fields to `shared/schema.ts`.
2. Run `npm --workspace @datafn/cli run generate -- --schema shared/schema.ts`.
3. Update `server/authz.ts` if the resource is restricted.
4. Add UI bindings via `client.table(...)`.
5. Write at least one integration test under `tests/integration/`.

## Docs
The full DataFn documentation is at https://datafn.21n.co/docs. Raw markdown for any page is at /api/docs/raw/<path>.mdx. For example: https://datafn.21n.co/api/docs/raw/dfql/mutations.mdx
```

### Skills

For multi-skill projects, drop individual files into `.claude/skills/`:

```
.claude/
├── skills/
│   ├── datafn-schema.md       (schema and capabilities)
│   ├── datafn-dfql.md         (writing queries and mutations)
│   ├── datafn-sync.md         (clone/pull/push semantics)
│   └── datafn-server.md       (authz, plugins, routes)
```

Each skill is a short Markdown file. Claude Code loads them based on the current task.

## Claude Desktop

Claude Desktop supports MCP servers via `claude_desktop_config.json`:

**macOS:** `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
**Windows:** `%APPDATA%/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "datafn": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/abs/path/to/datafn-mcp/index.js"]
    }
  }
}
```

After restart, Claude Desktop exposes the DataFn MCP tools as native skills. See [MCP](/docs/ai-resources/mcp) for the reference server.

## One-click open

The "Open in Claude" button on every documentation page constructs a deep link to `claude.ai/new?q=...` with a prompt that asks Claude to read the current page. No setup required for this — it works in the browser.

## Verifying it works

In Claude Code with a `CLAUDE.md` in place:

> "Add a `dueDate: timestamp` field to the `tasks` resource and update the relevant client UI."

Claude should:

1. Read `shared/schema.ts`.
2. Add the field with `type: "date"` (DataFn convention).
3. Re-run codegen.
4. Update the React/Svelte component without asking what `client.table("tasks")` is.

If Claude reaches for raw SQL or skips DFQL, your `CLAUDE.md` needs to be more explicit about conventions.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Codex / GPT-based assistants

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/ai-resources/codex
Description: Wire DataFn into OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Continue.dev.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

OpenAI Codex (and GPT-based assistants in general) discover project conventions through one of three mechanisms:

1. `AGENTS.md` at the repo root (Codex CLI).
2. Repo-level instructions on github.com (Copilot for GitHub).
3. `.continue/rules/*.md` (Continue.dev).

The content is largely the same. Below is a starter that works for any of them — drop it in and adjust paths.

## AGENTS.md starter

```md
# DataFn project

This repo uses DataFn for sync, queries, and mutations.

## Layout
- `shared/schema.ts` — source-of-truth DataFn schema, used by client and server.
- `server/` — TypeScript server using `@datafn/server` + Hono.
- `client/` — React app using `@datafn/client` + `@datafn/react` (if present).
- `mobile/` — Swift package using `@datafn/apple`.

## Tooling
- `npm test` runs the full test suite (server + client).
- `npm run generate:schema` regenerates Drizzle and TypeScript types from `shared/schema.ts`.
- `npm run validate:schema` enforces the schema is well-formed.

## DataFn conventions
- Add new resources via `defineSchema(...)` in `shared/schema.ts`.
- Wire authorization in `server/authz.ts`. The default `authorize` returns false; tighten, don't loosen.
- Client access is always through `client.table("<resource>").<verb>(...)`; never read or write IndexedDB directly.
- Wrap multi-step writes in `client.transact(...)`. Never fire more than one `mutate` in a single user action.
- Capability operations (`trash`, `restore`, `archive`, `unarchive`, `share`, `unshare`) are first-class. Use them; don't model them as boolean fields.

## When fixing bugs
1. Reproduce the failure with a deterministic test before fixing.
2. Check `server/src/execution/errors.ts` for the error code's classification.
3. If a new error code is needed, add it to `core/src/errors.ts` first, then update the server.

## Docs
See https://datafn.21n.co/docs. Raw markdown is at /api/docs/raw/<path>.mdx.
```

## GitHub Copilot

In repository settings → **Copilot** → **Code review** → **Custom instructions**, paste the same content. Copilot will use it for chat, code review, and PR summaries.

## Continue.dev

Continue reads rules from `.continue/rules/*.md`:

```
.continue/
└── rules/
    └── datafn.md
```

No frontmatter needed; Continue applies them to all chat sessions in the project.

## Open in ChatGPT

The "Open in ChatGPT" button on every doc page constructs a deep link to `chatgpt.com/?q=...` with a prompt that asks the model to read the current page. This works without any setup.

## Verifying it works

In a session with the rules in place:

> "Add `clonable` capability to the `templates` resource."

The assistant should:

1. Recognize that `clonable` is not a built-in DataFn capability.
2. Ask whether you want to model it as a plugin or a boolean field.
3. Reach for `defineSchema` and the plugin API rather than ad-hoc fields.

If it confidently adds `clonable` to the capabilities array as if it were built in, the rules need a "what capabilities exist" enumeration.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Cursor

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/ai-resources/cursor
Description: Wire DataFn into Cursor with project rules, raw-markdown lookups, and MCP.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This page covers three integrations Cursor users typically want when working in a DataFn codebase.

## 1. Project rules

Cursor reads `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` for codebase-wide guidance. Drop in a single rule file for DataFn:

```mdc
---
description: DataFn conventions
globs:
  - "**/*.ts"
  - "**/*.tsx"
  - "**/*.svelte"
alwaysApply: true
---

# DataFn

This project uses DataFn for the client/server data layer.

## Public surfaces
- `@datafn/core` — schema, DFQL types, error codes
- `@datafn/server` — HTTP routes, validation, sync engine
- `@datafn/client` — client envelope, signals, offline storage
- `@datafn/svelte` — Svelte adapter

## Rules
- All schema changes go through `defineSchema(...)` and `validateSchema(...)`.
- All client-side data access goes through `client.table(...)`. Never write to IndexedDB directly.
- Sync routes are mounted on `/datafn/*` and should not be wrapped in custom middleware. Cross-cutting concerns belong in the `authorize` callback or a server plugin.
- Errors travel as `DatafnEnvelope`. Surface `error.code` to the UI for routing; never show raw `error.message` to end users.

See the docs at https://datafn.21n.co/docs.
```

See the [Skills](/docs/ai-resources/skills) page for a fuller starter template.

## 2. Raw markdown for grounding

The "Open in Cursor" button on every page sends the page URL to Cursor's prompt panel. From there Cursor can fetch the raw markdown:

```
fetch https://datafn.21n.co/api/docs/raw/dfql/queries.mdx
```

Cursor also accepts `@docs` references in the chat panel. If you've added DataFn as a docs source (Cursor settings → Indexing → Docs → Add → `https://datafn.21n.co/docs`), every page is searchable as `@docs:datafn`.

## 3. MCP server

Cursor 0.43+ supports MCP servers. Register `datafn-mcp` in `.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "datafn": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["./tools/datafn-mcp/index.js"]
    }
  }
}
```

Once registered, the `search_docs`, `fetch_page`, `get_route`, and `get_error` tools become available to Cursor's agent mode. See the [MCP](/docs/ai-resources/mcp) page for the reference implementation.

## 4. Snippets

Save the following as `.cursor/snippets/datafn.json` to get quick scaffolds:

```json
{
  "DFQL Query": {
    "prefix": "dfquery",
    "body": [
      "const $1: DfqlQuery = {",
      "  resource: \"$2\",",
      "  version: 1,",
      "  filters: { $3 },",
      "  sort: [\"$4:desc\"],",
      "  limit: $5",
      "};"
    ]
  },
  "DFQL Mutation": {
    "prefix": "dfmutation",
    "body": [
      "const $1: DfqlMutation = {",
      "  resource: \"$2\",",
      "  version: 1,",
      "  operation: \"$3|insert,merge,replace,delete|\",",
      "  id: $4,",
      "  record: { $5 }",
      "};"
    ]
  }
}
```

## Verifying it works

Open a Cursor chat in a DataFn project and ask:

> "Show me how to define an `archivable` resource with `idPrefix: \"prj\"` and a `title` field."

You should see the assistant reach for `defineSchema` and reference `@datafn/core` without prompting.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### llms.txt / llms-full.txt

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/ai-resources/llms-txt
Description: Machine-readable artifacts that turn the DataFn documentation into a prompt-friendly corpus.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The DataFn docs site publishes two artifacts that follow the emerging [`llms.txt` convention](https://llmstxt.org/):

## llms.txt

A short outline of the site organized by section. Suitable for grounding a single prompt or seeding a retrieval index.

```
https://datafn.21n.co/llms.txt
```

Typical size: ~20–40 KB. Each entry is a Markdown bullet:

```
- [Schema Definition](https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/schema): Define and validate your DataFn schema, including capability-driven behavior.
```

The file is regenerated from `content/docs/**` on every build so it never drifts from the rendered site.

## llms-full.txt

The complete body of every page, concatenated with section separators and deep-link headers. Suitable for direct ingestion by long-context models, embeddings, or fine-tuning datasets.

```
https://datafn.21n.co/llms-full.txt
```

Typical size: 300–500 KB. Structure:

```
================================================================================
## Dfql
================================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Schema Definition

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/schema
Description: Define and validate your DataFn schema, including capability-driven behavior.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

(full markdown body of the page)
```

## Regenerating locally

The artifacts are generated at build time:

```bash
cd datafn/docs
npm run generate:llms
```

You can also override the base URL used in the generated links:

```bash
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://my-mirror.example.com npm run generate:llms
```

The script lives at `datafn/docs/scripts/generate-llms.mjs` — it walks `content/docs/`, parses frontmatter, and emits both files into `public/`.

## Per-page raw markdown

Beyond the two corpus files, every page is reachable as raw MDX:

```
GET /api/docs/raw/<path-to-page>.mdx
```

Example:

```bash
curl https://datafn.21n.co/api/docs/raw/dfql/filters.mdx
```

The "Copy Markdown" button at the top of every page uses this endpoint behind the scenes.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### MCP Server (Experimental)

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/ai-resources/mcp
Description: Expose the DataFn documentation and schema as Model Context Protocol tools for agentic clients.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) is a JSON-RPC protocol that lets LLM clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, agentic frameworks) discover and call tools. The DataFn project ships a minimal MCP server that exposes the documentation and the live HTTP surface as tools.

## Suggested tools to expose

A working DataFn MCP server typically registers four tools:

| Tool | Inputs | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `search_docs` | `query: string`, optional `section: string` | Top N pages with title, URL, and a snippet. |
| `fetch_page` | `path: string` | Raw markdown body of the requested page. |
| `get_route` | `method: string`, `path: string` | Request/response schema and error codes for an HTTP route. |
| `get_error` | `code: string` (e.g. `DFQL_INVALID`) | Description, common causes, and fix suggestions. |

Optional extras:

- `list_resources` — enumerate resources, fields, and capabilities from a running DataFn server's `/datafn/status`.
- `run_query` — execute a read-only DFQL query against a developer instance (only behind a feature flag).

## Reference implementation

A minimal Node.js implementation that wraps the static documentation and the running server:

```typescript
import { McpServer, StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server";

const docsRoot = "https://datafn.21n.co";

const server = new McpServer({ name: "datafn-docs", version: "0.1.0" });

server.tool(
  "search_docs",
  { query: { type: "string" } },
  async ({ query }) => {
    const llms = await fetch(`${docsRoot}/llms.txt`).then((r) => r.text());
    const matches = llms
      .split("\n")
      .filter((line) => line.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()))
      .slice(0, 10);
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text: matches.join("\n") }] };
  },
);

server.tool(
  "fetch_page",
  { path: { type: "string" } },
  async ({ path }) => {
    const md = await fetch(`${docsRoot}/api/docs/raw/${path}`).then((r) => r.text());
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text: md }] };
  },
);

await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport());
```

## Wiring it into clients

### Claude Desktop

Add the server to `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "datafn": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/path/to/datafn-mcp/index.js"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Cursor

Cursor reads MCP servers from `.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "datafn": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/path/to/datafn-mcp/index.js"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Other agentic frameworks

Any MCP-compatible client (LangChain, LlamaIndex via plugins, OpenAI's Responses API in beta) can target the same stdio or HTTP transport.

## Hosting the MCP server

The reference implementation runs over stdio, which works well for local tools. For team use you can wrap the same handlers in an HTTP transport and host on Cloudflare Workers, Fly.io, or your existing infrastructure. The handlers are pure functions of the documentation and the running server's status, so they can run anywhere there's outbound HTTP access.

## Roadmap

Planned additions: `get_schema` (return the resolved schema from a target deployment), `simulate_mutation` (dry-run a mutation through validation), `explain_query` (return the parsed AST for a DFQL query). Open an issue if your agent needs a tool that isn't listed.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Skills

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/ai-resources/skills
Description: Drop-in instruction files that teach AI coding assistants how to use DataFn correctly.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A "skill" is a short instruction file you commit alongside your code that teaches an AI coding assistant the local conventions for working with DataFn. Each assistant has its own location and format:

| Assistant | Location | Format |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cursor | `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` | MDC (Markdown with frontmatter) |
| Claude Code | `CLAUDE.md` at project root, or `.claude/skills/*` | Plain Markdown |
| OpenAI Codex | `AGENTS.md` at project root | Plain Markdown |
| Continue.dev | `.continue/rules/*.md` | Markdown |

The content can be largely the same across formats. Below is a starter that works for any DataFn project. Tailor the schema and conventions to your codebase.

## Starter skill

```md
# DataFn project conventions

## Stack
- Server: TypeScript via `@datafn/server` mounted on Hono
- Client (web): `@datafn/client` with `@datafn/svelte` adapter
- Client (mobile): `@datafn/apple` via Swift package
- Database: Postgres via `@superfunctions/db` Drizzle adapter
- Auth: `@authfn/server` provides the session; namespaceProvider derives `ns(orgId, userId)`

## Schema rules
- Always declare resources via `defineSchema(...)` from `@datafn/core` so capability declarations are type-checked.
- Default capabilities: `["timestamps", "audit"]` at the schema level. Add `archivable`, `trashable`, `shareable` only when needed.
- Field naming: camelCase. ID prefix is the first 3 letters of the resource name (e.g. `prj` for `projects`).
- Indices: declare `base` indices for every field that appears in a filter or sort; `search` indices for full-text fields.

## DFQL rules
- Prefer `select` projections; never request all fields from large resources.
- Use cursor pagination (`cursor`) over offset for any list with >100 items.
- Wrap multi-step writes in a transaction; never call multiple mutations from the client without `transact`.
- `metadata.includeTrashed` and `includeArchived` default to false; only set to true with explicit user intent.

## Authorization
- Field-level authz lives in `server/authz.ts`. New resources must add a policy entry there.
- `authorize()` returns `false` by default. Tighten, don't loosen.
- Always pair sharing with audit logging (it's a hard dependency in the schema).

## What to avoid
- Don't bypass the client envelope (`{ ok, result }`/`{ ok, error }`). Surface errors to the UI from `result.error.code`.
- Don't write to underlying tables directly — go through DFQL so capabilities, sync, and authz fire correctly.
- Don't use `replace` when `merge` will do. `replace` overwrites all fields including capability-managed ones.

## When in doubt
1. Read the DataFn docs at https://datafn.21n.co/docs (raw markdown at /api/docs/raw/<path>).
2. Use the MCP server (`datafn-mcp`) if it's registered.
3. Ask the user before introducing a new capability, plugin, or sync route.
```

## Where to put it

### Cursor

```
my-project/
└── .cursor/
    └── rules/
        └── datafn.mdc
```

Frontmatter for Cursor:

```mdc
---
description: DataFn conventions for this project
globs:
  - "src/**/*.ts"
  - "src/**/*.tsx"
  - "src/**/*.svelte"
alwaysApply: true
---

# DataFn project conventions
...
```

### Claude Code

```
my-project/
└── CLAUDE.md
```

Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` automatically; no frontmatter required.

### OpenAI Codex

```
my-project/
└── AGENTS.md
```

Codex auto-discovers `AGENTS.md` at the repo root.

## Tips

- Keep skills under ~200 lines. Long skills hurt context.
- Pin to a DataFn version: "We are on `@datafn/server` 0.3.x" prevents the assistant from suggesting deprecated APIs.
- Link out to the docs. `See https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/mutations` is better than inlining all the rules.
- Re-read the skill on major refactors. Stale skills mislead agents harder than no skills at all.

### AI Resources

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/ai-resources
Description: LLM-ready artifacts and agent affordances for working with DataFn through Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, and other assistants.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This documentation site is built to be consumed by AI assistants as well as people. Every page exposes raw markdown and one-click handoff to popular chat UIs so an agent can pick up where you left off.

## What's available

- **`llms.txt`** — short table of contents with deep links, suitable for grounding a prompt or a retrieval index.
- **`llms-full.txt`** — the full content of every documentation page, optimized for direct ingestion by language models.
- **Per-page "Open in" buttons** — every page ships with a Popover that hands the current URL to ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, or Scira.
- **Raw markdown endpoint** — `GET /api/docs/raw/<path>` serves the unrendered MDX behind any page.
- **MCP server (experimental)** — expose `search_docs`, `fetch_page`, `get_route`, and `get_error` to MCP-compatible clients.
- **Editor skills** — drop-in instruction files for Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex.

## When to use which artifact

| You want to... | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Ground a model on the public surface of DataFn in 20K tokens | [`llms.txt`](/docs/ai-resources/llms-txt) |
| Train or fine-tune on the entire corpus | [`llms-full.txt`](/docs/ai-resources/llms-txt) |
| Let your IDE answer "how do I use this" without copying anything | [Cursor rules](/docs/ai-resources/cursor) / [Claude skills](/docs/ai-resources/claude) / [Codex instructions](/docs/ai-resources/codex) |
| Wire DataFn into an agentic tool with structured search | [MCP server](/docs/ai-resources/mcp) |
| Hand off the current page to ChatGPT/Claude/Cursor | Use the **Open** button at the top of any page |

## Quick sanity check

You can verify the artifacts are live from the command line:

```bash
curl https://datafn.21n.co/llms.txt | head -50
curl https://datafn.21n.co/llms-full.txt | wc -c
curl https://datafn.21n.co/api/docs/raw/dfql/queries.mdx | head -30
```

If you're self-hosting these docs the same URLs work against your own deployment.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### CLI Overview

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli
Description: Command-line tools for DataFn schema management and code generation.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Overview

The `@datafn/cli` package provides command-line tools for validating DataFn schemas and generating TypeScript types and database schema files from them.

```bash
npm install -D @datafn/cli
```

## Available Commands

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `datafn generate` | Generate TypeScript types and database schemas from your schema file. |
| `datafn validate` | Validate your schema file structure and integrity. |

## Schema Auto-Discovery

When no `--schema` flag is provided, the CLI searches for schema files in the following order:

1. `schema.datafn.ts`
2. `src/schema.datafn.ts`
3. `schema.json`
4. `src/schema.json`

The first file found is used.

## Schema File Formats

### TypeScript (`.datafn.ts`)

TypeScript schema files export a schema object built with `defineSchema()`:

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export default defineSchema({
  resources: [
    {
      name: "todos",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "td",
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "completed", type: "boolean", required: true },
      ],
    },
  ],
});
```

### JSON (`.json`)

JSON schema files use the same structure without the `defineSchema` wrapper:

```json
{
  "resources": [
    {
      "name": "todos",
      "version": 1,
      "idPrefix": "td",
      "fields": [
        { "name": "title", "type": "string", "required": true },
        { "name": "completed", "type": "boolean", "required": true }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Both formats are validated identically at load time using `validateSchema()` from `@datafn/core`.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Comparison

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/comparison
Description: Where DataFn sits relative to Replicache, ElectricSQL, PowerSync, RxDB, WatermelonDB, InstantDB, Convex, TinyBase, and a Drizzle+TanStack Query stack.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This page exists so you can quickly decide whether DataFn is the right tool for your problem — and where it isn't. The short version: DataFn is a self-hosted, schema-first, offline-capable data layer with built-in capabilities (sharing, audit, soft-delete) and an extensible query language. If you want managed backend-as-a-service (Firebase / Convex / InstantDB), DataFn is the wrong shape. If you want a thin sync layer over your own Postgres with native iOS support, it's the right one.

## When to reach for DataFn

- You own your backend and want to keep owning it (no SaaS lock-in).
- You need offline-first with multi-device sync and you don't want to write the conflict resolution yourself.
- You want capabilities (trash, archive, share, audit) as first-class declarations, not bespoke boolean fields.
- Your client surface includes native iOS/macOS, not just web.
- You want a schema-first contract where the same definition drives types, validation, sync, and (optionally) ORM tables.

## When DataFn is the wrong fit

- You want a serverless backend you don't manage (use **Convex**, **InstantDB**, **Firebase**).
- You're only on web and you're happy with TanStack Query + raw fetch.
- You need full SQL on the client (use **PowerSync** or **ElectricSQL** with a SQLite-shaped client API).
- You want CRDTs with arbitrary ordering and partial-state replication (use **Automerge**, **Yjs**, or **Liveblocks**).
- Your data is read-mostly and a static export plus revalidation is enough.

## At a glance

| | DataFn | Replicache | ElectricSQL | PowerSync | RxDB | WatermelonDB | InstantDB | Convex | TinyBase | Drizzle + TanStack Query |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Backend** | Self-hosted (Node or Python) | Self-hosted | Self-hosted | Self-hosted | BYO | BYO | Managed | Managed | None / BYO | Self-hosted |
| **Offline-first** | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Limited | Limited | Yes (in memory) | No (without extra work) |
| **Native iOS / macOS** | First-class (CoreData) | No | No | Yes (Kotlin/Swift) | Web/RN | RN, native bridges | No | No | Web only | No |
| **Query language** | DFQL (JSON) | KV scan via JS | SQL | SQL | Mongo-like | Lokijs / custom | InstaQL | Document store | None | SQL |
| **Schema-first** | Yes | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Optional | Yes |
| **Built-in sharing/ACL** | Yes (`shareable` capability) | No | No | No | No | No | Yes | Limited | No | No |
| **Built-in soft-delete/audit** | Yes (capabilities) | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | Manual |
| **Multi-tenancy primitives** | Yes (namespaces) | No | Manual | Manual | Manual | Manual | Limited | Limited | No | Manual |
| **REST auto-generation** | Yes (opt-in) | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No |
| **Pluggable search** | Yes (provider interface) | No | Manual | Manual | Yes (lite) | Yes (lite) | Yes | Yes | No | Manual |
| **Live updates (WS)** | Yes | Yes (poke) | Yes | Yes | Yes (via plugin) | Yes (via plugin) | Yes | Yes | No | Manual |
| **Mature LLM tooling** | Yes (llms.txt, MCP) | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No |

A `Yes` in the table means "shipped in the box without writing custom code"; a `Manual` means "possible but you build it".

## Detailed comparisons

### vs Replicache

Replicache is a great choice when you want a thin "client-server sync with a server you control" and you'll build everything else yourself.

- **Schema:** Replicache is schema-less (key/value records keyed by ID + an opaque value). DataFn requires a schema; you get type safety for free, plus capability-driven behaviour.
- **Query language:** Replicache asks you to write JavaScript scans for every read. DataFn ships DFQL, which is JSON in/JSON out and identical on client and server.
- **Server work:** Replicache's server is "all yours" — you implement `push` and `pull` from scratch. DataFn ships them.
- **Sharing/ACL:** Replicache is BYO; DataFn ships `shareable` + per-resource policies.
- **Native:** Replicache is web-only. DataFn ships an Apple runtime.

If you want full control of the wire protocol and you're going to build sharing yourself anyway, Replicache wins on minimalism. If you want batteries, DataFn wins.

### vs ElectricSQL

ElectricSQL replicates a Postgres shape into a local SQLite. You write SQL on both sides.

- **Mental model:** ElectricSQL is "Postgres on the client". DataFn is "a typed query language with sync, capabilities, and an optional REST surface".
- **Schema flexibility:** ElectricSQL ties you to a specific Postgres dialect. DataFn abstracts the database so you can run on Postgres, SQLite, MySQL, or D1.
- **Built-in capabilities:** ElectricSQL doesn't model sharing, soft-delete, or audit. You add columns yourself.
- **Native:** ElectricSQL has Swift bindings via SQLite; DataFn ships a CoreData-backed runtime that integrates with SwiftUI's observation system.
- **Migration story:** ElectricSQL relies on Postgres logical replication. DataFn uses a server-side sequence store and incremental cursors.

If your team is deeply invested in SQL on every layer, ElectricSQL fits. If you want a JSON-shaped query language with capabilities, DataFn fits.

### vs PowerSync

PowerSync also replicates Postgres → SQLite, with strong support for native iOS, Android, and React Native.

- **Native support:** PowerSync's native story is strong. DataFn's iOS/macOS story is also strong but is CoreData-based rather than SQLite-based. If your existing iOS app uses CoreData, DataFn fits naturally.
- **Server topology:** PowerSync runs as a managed service or self-hosted gateway in front of your Postgres. DataFn runs inside your existing HTTP server.
- **Pricing model:** PowerSync has a paid tier for hosted infrastructure. DataFn is OSS, no hosted offering.

### vs RxDB

RxDB is a TypeScript-only client-side database with optional sync plugins.

- **Server:** RxDB asks you to bring or write a server. DataFn ships one.
- **Native:** RxDB runs in React Native via a SQLite adapter; DataFn's native runtime is purpose-built for SwiftUI.
- **Sharing/ACL:** Manual in RxDB; first-class in DataFn.
- **Query language:** RxDB uses a Mongo-like query language. DataFn uses DFQL — similar shape, but with explicit field-level authz and aggregation primitives.

### vs WatermelonDB

WatermelonDB is the Lego-block local database for React Native, with manual sync.

- **Sync:** WatermelonDB ships a sync API but doesn't ship a server. DataFn ships both.
- **Web:** WatermelonDB on web is uncommon; DataFn's web story is first-class.
- **Capabilities:** Manual in WatermelonDB.

### vs InstantDB

InstantDB is a managed backend with a graph-shaped data model.

- **Hosting:** InstantDB is SaaS. DataFn is self-hosted.
- **Data model:** InstantDB is graph-shaped (triples). DataFn is relational with capabilities.
- **iOS:** InstantDB is web-first. DataFn ships a native runtime.

### vs Convex

Convex is a managed backend with functions, queries, and real-time subscriptions.

- **Hosting:** Convex is SaaS. DataFn is self-hosted.
- **Language:** Convex queries are TS functions on the server; DataFn queries are JSON DFQL that run on the client and server.
- **Mental model:** Convex feels like Firebase rewritten for TypeScript devs. DataFn feels like a schema-first ORM that happens to sync.

### vs TinyBase

TinyBase is a strict client-only reactive state store.

- **Server:** TinyBase has none. DataFn ships one.
- **Sync:** TinyBase has persistence plugins but no server-coordinated sync. DataFn's sync engine is the point.

### vs Drizzle + TanStack Query

The default React/Vue/Svelte stack: Drizzle on the server, TanStack Query on the client, REST or tRPC in between.

- **Offline:** This stack does not give you offline writes. DataFn does.
- **Sharing/ACL:** You build it. DataFn ships it.
- **Native:** Not in scope. DataFn ships an iOS runtime.
- **DX:** TanStack Query is a great query cache but does not understand your schema. DataFn understands the schema and uses it for sync, validation, and codegen.

Use Drizzle + TanStack Query if you don't need offline and you want the smallest, simplest stack. Use DataFn when you need offline sync, multi-device, native iOS, or capabilities like sharing and audit.

## Migration tips

- **From Replicache** → reuse your existing push/pull endpoints by mounting them at `/replicache/*` and gradually move resources behind `/datafn/*`.
- **From ElectricSQL** → keep Postgres as your database, swap the client layer in stages, resource by resource.
- **From TanStack Query** → start with a single resource and migrate incrementally; the DataFn client can co-exist with your existing fetch logic.
- **From InstantDB / Convex** → expect to redesign the data model; capability-driven schemas are usually a simplification, not a translation.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### DFQL Overview

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql
Description: DataFn Query Language - a JSON-based query and mutation language.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DFQL (DataFn Query Language) is a structured, JSON-based language for querying and mutating data. Every operation -- whether reading a single record, filtering a large dataset, or executing a multi-step transaction -- is expressed as a plain JSON object with well-defined fields.

## Design Principles

DFQL is designed around three core principles:

- **Uniform envelope pattern.** Queries, mutations, and transactions all share a common shape: a `resource` and `version` to identify the target, plus operation-specific fields.
- **Isomorphic execution.** The same DFQL objects are used by both the client and server. A query written for the client executes identically on the server, enabling offline-first architectures with no translation layer.
- **Composable operations.** Filters, sorting, pagination, select projections, and aggregations can be combined freely within a single query.

## Operation Types

DFQL supports three top-level operation types:

### Queries

Retrieve data from a resource. Queries support filtering, sorting, pagination, field selection, aggregation, [timezone-aware temporal filtering and grouping](/docs/dfql/temporal), and full-text search.

```typescript
const query: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  filters: { completed: false },
  sort: ["priority:desc"],
  limit: 20,
};
```

### Mutations

Create, update, or delete records. Mutations support core operations (`insert`, `merge`, `replace`, `delete`), capability operations (`trash`, `restore`, `archive`, `unarchive`, `share`, `unshare`), relation management, conditional guards, and debounced writes.

```typescript
const mutation: DfqlMutation = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  operation: "insert",
  record: { title: "Buy groceries", completed: false },
};
```

### Transactions

Execute a sequence of queries and mutations as an atomic unit. If any step fails, all preceding mutations are rolled back.

```typescript
const transaction: DfqlTransact = {
  atomic: true,
  steps: [
    { mutation: { resource: "accounts", version: 1, operation: "merge", id: "acc_1", record: { balance: 900 } } },
    { mutation: { resource: "accounts", version: 1, operation: "merge", id: "acc_2", record: { balance: 1100 } } },
  ],
};
```

## Type Definitions

All DFQL types are exported from `@datafn/core`:

```typescript
import type {
  DfqlQuery,
  DfqlMutation,
  DfqlTransact,
  DfqlSort,
  DfqlCursor,
} from "@datafn/core";
```

The `DfqlQueryFragment` and `DfqlMutationFragment` types omit the `resource` and `version` fields, which are useful when working through client table handles that inject those fields automatically.

Capability semantics are schema-driven. See [Capabilities](/docs/documentation/capabilities).

## Normalization and Caching

DFQL objects can be normalized to a canonical form for use as cache keys:

```typescript
import { normalizeDfql, dfqlKey } from "@datafn/core";

// Canonical JSON representation (sorted keys, stripped undefined)
const normalized = normalizeDfql(query);

// Stable string key for caching
const key = dfqlKey(query);
```

`normalizeDfql` recursively sorts object keys alphabetically, strips `undefined` values, and preserves `null`. `dfqlKey` produces a deterministic JSON string from the normalized form.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Overview

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/documentation
Description: What DataFn is, what it ships, and how the pieces fit together.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What is DataFn?

DataFn is a **full-stack data framework**. You define your data model once, mount a set of route handlers on the backend you already have, and drop a client into your web or native app. From there you get type-safe queries and mutations, offline-first local storage, real-time sync, multi-tenant isolation, and per-record sharing — without bolting together an ORM, a query client, a sync layer, and a websocket stack yourself.

If you've ever found yourself writing `useEffect → fetch → setState → invalidate cache → handle offline → handle conflicts → handle realtime` in your apps, that's the surface area DataFn collapses.

## When DataFn is a good fit

- Apps where users care about **working offline** (mobile-first, PWAs, native).
- Apps with **collaborative or shared data** (per-record sharing, multi-tenant SaaS).
- Apps that need **live updates** between users or devices.
- Apps where you want **typed end-to-end** schemas without hand-syncing types between client and server.

If your app is a stateless CRUD form over a single Postgres database with no offline or realtime story, a plain ORM and `fetch` will probably do.

## How the pieces fit together

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Web ["Web Client (Browser)"]
        DC[DatafnClient]
        SIG[Signals]
        STR["Storage — IndexedDB / Memory"]
        SV[Svelte Adapter]
    end

    subgraph Apple ["Native Client (iOS / macOS)"]
        AR[DatafnAppleRuntime]
        SUI[SwiftUI Bindings]
        CDS[CoreData Store]
        CK[CloudKit Sync]
    end

    subgraph Protocol ["DFQL Protocol"]
        Q[Queries]
        M[Mutations]
        T[Transactions]
        LIVE["Live — WebSocket Cursors"]
    end

    subgraph Server ["Server (Node.js / Python)"]
        DS[DatafnServer]
        RT["Routes — DFQL / REST"]
        AUTH["Authorization — Namespaces, Sharing, Capabilities"]
        SE[Sync Engine]
        SEQ["Sequence Store — Redis / KV / DB"]
        WSB[WebSocket Broadcaster]
        PL[Plugins & Search Providers]
    end

    subgraph DB ["Database"]
        AD["Adapters — Drizzle / SQLAlchemy"]
        PG[(PostgreSQL / SQLite)]
    end

    DC --> SIG
    SIG --> SV
    DC --> STR
    DC <-->|"clone / pull / push"| SE
    DC <-->|"query / mutate / transact"| RT
    DC <-.->|live| WSB

    AR --> SUI
    AR --> CDS
    AR <--> CK
    AR <-->|"clone / pull / push"| SE
    AR <-->|"query / mutate / transact"| RT
    AR <-.->|live| WSB

    RT --> AUTH
    RT --> DS
    RT --> PL
    DS --> AD
    SE --> SEQ
    SE --> AD
    AD --> PG
```

The **schema** in the middle (not shown) is the contract every layer agrees on — defined once, imported by both client and server.

## Packages

DataFn is split into small packages so you only install what you actually use.

### Shared

| Package | Language | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@datafn/core` | TypeScript | Schema definition (`defineSchema`), DFQL types, capability primitives. Imported by both client and server. |

### Server

| Package | Language | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@datafn/server` | TypeScript | `createDatafnServer()` — handlers for query / mutation / transact / sync, plus optional auto-generated REST and WebSocket broadcaster. Mount on Hono, Express, Bun, or anything fetch-compatible. |
| `datafn` (PyPI) | Python | `create_datafn_server()` — same handler surface for FastAPI / Starlette / Flask, backed by SQLAlchemy. |

### Web client

| Package | Language | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@datafn/client` | TypeScript | `createDatafnClient()` — local storage (IndexedDB or memory), sync engine, reactive signals, optional WebSocket live updates. Framework-agnostic. |
| `@datafn/svelte` | TypeScript | Converts DataFn signals into Svelte readable stores. Other framework adapters (React, Vue, Solid, Angular) are planned but not yet shipped. |

### Native client (Apple)

| Package | Language | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DatafnAppleRuntime` | Swift | Same client model as `@datafn/client`, but native: CoreData-backed local store, async actor runtime, observation source for reactive reads. |
| `DatafnSwiftUI` | Swift | `@Observable @MainActor` query bindings (`DatafnObservedQuery`) that drop straight into SwiftUI views. |
| `DatafnCoreDataStore` | Swift | The CoreData persistence layer used by the runtime. |
| `DatafnServerSync` | Swift | Talks to a `@datafn/server` over HTTP + WebSocket — equivalent to the web client's sync. |
| `DatafnCloudKitSync` | Swift | Alternative sync backend that uses CloudKit's private database instead of a DataFn server. |
| `DatafnWebViewBridgeHost` | Swift | Lets a `WKWebView` running `@datafn/client` share storage and sync with the native runtime. |

The Apple runtime targets **iOS 17+ and macOS 14+** and is distributed via Swift Package Manager.

### CLI

| Package | Language | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@datafn/cli` | TypeScript | Schema validation and codegen — generates Drizzle table definitions and TypeScript types from your schema. |

## Core concepts

A short tour of the ideas you'll meet next. Each links to a deeper page.

### DFQL — DataFn Query Language

DFQL is a structured JSON protocol that describes every read and write. Both client and server speak it, so the wire format and the API surface match. DFQL covers:

- [**Schema**](/docs/dfql/schema) — typed resources, fields, indices, and relations.
- [**Queries**](/docs/dfql/queries) — filters, sorting, pagination, field selection, aggregations.
- [**Mutations**](/docs/dfql/mutations) — `insert`, `merge`, `replace`, `delete`, plus capability ops (`trash`, `restore`, `archive`, `unarchive`, `share`, `unshare`).
- [**Transactions**](/docs/dfql/transactions) — multiple operations executed atomically.

### Capabilities

Capabilities are **opt-in behaviors you switch on per resource**. Turn one on and DataFn injects the relevant system fields, exposes the matching operations on the client, and enforces the rules on the server:

- `timestamps` adds `createdAt` / `updatedAt`.
- `audit` adds `createdBy` / `updatedBy`.
- `trash` enables soft-delete via `trash()` / `restore()`.
- `archivable` adds `archive()` / `unarchive()`.
- `shareable` enables per-record sharing.

This keeps boilerplate (timestamps, soft-delete, audit trails) out of your application code. See [Capabilities](/docs/documentation/capabilities) for the full list.

### Offline-first sync

Every read and write goes through local storage first; the network is opportunistic. DataFn's sync engine moves changes between client and server in five distinct phases:

- **Clone** — initial full download of a resource.
- **Pull** — incremental download of changes since the last sync.
- **Push** — upload locally queued mutations.
- **Reconcile** — merge server-authoritative state back into local storage.
- **CloneUp** — bulk upload (mainly for native clients seeding a fresh server).

See [Offline-First Sync](/docs/documentation/sync/offline-first) for the full lifecycle.

### Real-time

The server can broadcast cursor invalidations over WebSocket, namespace-scoped and targeted at the relevant principals — so other tabs, devices, and users see fresh data without polling. See [WebSockets](/docs/documentation/server/websockets).

### Namespaces (multi-tenancy)

Row-level [namespace isolation](/docs/documentation/namespaces) is on by default. Every record carries a `__ns` column, every query is auto-scoped, and there's no way to accidentally read across tenants. You provide a `namespaceProvider` on the server (typically derived from the authenticated user's session) and DataFn handles the rest.

### Sharing

Beyond namespaces, DataFn ships a [sharing model](/docs/documentation/sharing) for collaborative apps: grant access to specific users or principals, scope the grant by relation, and let the server enforce visibility automatically.

### Plugins

Pre/post hooks on `query`, `mutation`, and `sync` flows let you add custom logic — encryption at rest, audit logging, derived fields, third-party search providers — without forking the framework. See [Plugins](/docs/documentation/plugins/overview).

## Where to next

- New here? Walk through the [Getting Started](/docs/getting-started) guide — it gets you a server, schema, and client running end-to-end.
- Ready to design your data model? Start with [Schema](/docs/dfql/schema) and [Resources](/docs/dfql/schema/resources).
- Building a UI? See [Client Setup](/docs/documentation/client/setup) and [Signals](/docs/documentation/client/signals).
- Wiring up the backend? See [Server Setup](/docs/documentation/server/setup).

### Examples

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/examples
Description: Working reference apps that ship with DataFn — clone, run, copy what you need.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The repository ships three reference apps. They're not toys — they're how the maintainers exercise the core capabilities end-to-end. Use them as a starting point for your own architecture decisions.

| Example | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| [Todo app](/docs/examples/todo-app) | Minimum viable app with three deployment topologies (browser-owned, native-backed via WebView, native + CloudKit). |
| [Sharing app](/docs/examples/sharing-app) | Multi-actor, multi-workspace sharing semantics with deterministic E2E tests. |
| [Apple WebView host](/docs/examples/apple-webview-host) | The Swift host that demonstrates the native-backed and CloudKit topologies. |

All three examples live in `datafn/examples/` in the [super-functions repo](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions). Each has its own `README.md` with the canonical run instructions.

## Running them locally

Clone the repo and pick an example:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions
cd super-functions
npm install
```

Then follow the per-example walkthrough.

## What to learn from each

- **Todo app** is the right starting point for understanding how DataFn handles the same app across three topologies. Pay attention to how it switches between `IndexedDbStorageAdapter` and `createNativeBackedStorageAdapter` based on injected globals.
- **Sharing app** is the right reference for any product that needs per-record ACLs and deterministic E2E tests of share lifecycles.
- **Apple WebView host** is the right starting point for a Swift app that embeds a web view but wants native CoreData persistence and SearchFn indexing.

## Beyond the examples

If you want recipe-shaped walkthroughs (single-page recipes that ship with a working schema + server + client), see the [Recipes](/docs/recipes) section.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Getting Started

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/getting-started
Description: Get up and running with DataFn in minutes.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

import { Tab, Tabs } from "fumadocs-ui/components/tabs";

DataFn has two halves that talk to each other: a set of **route handlers** you mount on your backend, and a **client** that runs in the browser (or a native app) with an optional offline-first storage. They share one **schema**, so types and validation stay in sync end-to-end.

This guide walks through a minimal end-to-end setup.

## 1. Add DataFn to your backend

DataFn plugs into the backend you already have. You give it a database adapter and a schema, and it hands you back route handlers (`/datafn/query`, `/datafn/mutation`, `/datafn/sync/*`, etc.) that you mount on your existing app: Hono, Express, Bun, FastAPI, Starlette, anything that speaks HTTP.

Install the DataFn packages alongside your current backend dependencies:

<Tabs items={["TypeScript", "Python"]}>
  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    ```bash
    npm install @datafn/server @datafn/core
    ```

    `@datafn/core` holds the shared primitives (schema definition, types, query language) used by both client and server.

    `createDatafnServer()` validates your schema, wires up a database adapter, and returns a `router` you mount on your HTTP framework. Here it is mounted on Hono via the `@superfunctions/http-hono` adapter — equivalent helpers exist for Express and other frameworks:

    ```typescript
    import { Hono } from "hono";
    import { createDatafnServer } from "@datafn/server";
    import { drizzleAdapter } from "@superfunctions/db/adapters";
    import { toHono } from "@superfunctions/http-hono";
    import { schema } from "./schema"; // we'll define this in step 2

    const app = new Hono(); // your existing app

    const datafn = await createDatafnServer({
      schema,
      database: drizzleAdapter({ db: drizzleInstance, dialect: "postgres" }),
      rest: true, // also exposes a REST API auto-generated from your schema
    });

    // Mount DataFn's routes onto your existing Hono app
    app.route("/", toHono(datafn.router));

    export default app;
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab value="Python">
    ```bash
    pip install datafn
    ```

    `create_datafn_server()` validates your schema and returns a dictionary of route handlers keyed by `"METHOD /path"`. You wire those handlers into your existing FastAPI / Starlette / Flask app — DataFn doesn't run its own web server:

    ```python
    from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
    from datafn import create_datafn_server
    from .schema import schema  # we'll define this in step 2

    app = FastAPI()  # your existing app

    datafn = create_datafn_server({
        "schema": schema,
        "db": my_db_adapter,         # SQLAlchemy-based adapter
        "authorize": my_authorize_fn,
    })

    # Mount DataFn's handlers on your existing routes
    @app.post("/datafn/query")
    async def datafn_query(request: Request):
        ctx = {"user": request.state.user}
        return await datafn["routes"]["POST /datafn/query"](ctx, await request.json())

    @app.post("/datafn/mutation")
    async def datafn_mutation(request: Request):
        ctx = {"user": request.state.user}
        return await datafn["routes"]["POST /datafn/mutation"](ctx, await request.json())
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

That's the minimum. For production you'll add `authorize`, `namespaceProvider` (multi-tenancy), and `rateLimit` — see [Server Setup](/docs/documentation/server/setup).

## 2. Define your schema

The schema is the single source of truth for what data exists and how it behaves. Define it once in a shared file (e.g. `schema.ts`) and import it from both server and client:

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export const schema = defineSchema({
  // Capabilities add system fields and built-in operations to every resource:
  // - timestamps → adds createdAt, updatedAt
  // - audit      → adds createdBy, updatedBy
  // - trash      → enables soft-delete via trash() / restore()
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit", "trash"],
  resources: [
    {
      name: "tasks",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "tsk", // every row gets an id like "tsk:abc123"
      capabilities: ["archivable"], // adds archive() / unarchive() to tasks
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "completed", type: "boolean", required: true, default: false },
        { name: "priority", type: "number", required: false, min: 1, max: 5 },
      ],
      // Indices make these fields fast to filter and sort on.
      indices: { base: ["title", "completed", "priority"] },
    },
  ],
  relations: [],
});
```

DataFn uses this to generate types, validate inputs, drive sync, and (with the CLI) generate ORM (Drizzle/Prisma/Kysely) table definitions.

## 3. Set up the client

The client runs in the user's browser or a native iOS/macOS app. It stores data locally for offline use, syncs with the server in the background, and exposes a reactive API for your UI.

<Tabs items={["TypeScript", "Swift"]}>
  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    Install the client and core packages:

    ```bash
    npm install @datafn/client @datafn/core
    ```

    Create a client with `createDatafnClient()`. Point it at your server, give it a storage adapter, and pass the same schema you defined in step 2:

    ```typescript
    import { createDatafnClient, IndexedDbStorageAdapter } from "@datafn/client";
    import { schema } from "./schema";

    const client = createDatafnClient({
      schema,
      clientId: "device-1", // a stable id for this device — used to dedupe sync
      storage: new IndexedDbStorageAdapter("my-app-db"), // persistent local storage
      sync: {
        remote: "http://localhost:3000/datafn",
        offlinability: true, // queue mutations while offline, replay when back online
        ws: true,            // open a WebSocket for live updates from other clients
      },
    });
    ```

    For tests or short-lived sessions, swap `IndexedDbStorageAdapter` for `MemoryStorageAdapter`.
  </Tab>
  <Tab value="Swift">
    Add the DataFn Apple package via Swift Package Manager (in `Package.swift` or Xcode → Add Packages):

    ```swift
    .package(url: "https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions", from: "0.1.0"),
    // then depend on the product:
    .product(name: "DatafnAppleRuntime", package: "super-functions"),
    ```

    The Swift runtime is the equivalent of `createDatafnClient`: it owns a CoreData store for local persistence and talks to your DataFn server over HTTP and WebSocket. Pass it the same schema you defined in step 2 (exported as JSON — typically generated from your TS schema and bundled with the app):

    ```swift
    import DatafnAppleRuntime

    let configuration = DatafnAppleRuntimeConfiguration(
      schemaJSON: schemaData,         // Data loaded from a bundled schema.json
      schemaHash: "my-app-schema-v1", // bump when the schema changes
      namespace: "org-1:user-1",
      clientID: "device-1",           // stable per-device id, used to dedupe sync
      storeRootURL: FileManager.default
        .applicationSupportDirectory
        .appendingPathComponent("datafn-store", isDirectory: true),
      syncBackend: .datafnServer(
        DatafnServerSyncConfiguration(
          baseURL: URL(string: "http://localhost:3000/datafn")!,
          websocketURL: URL(string: "ws://localhost:3000/datafn/ws")!,
          profileID: "default"
        )
      )
    )

    let runtime = try await DatafnAppleRuntime(configuration: configuration)
    try await runtime.start()
    ```

    Prefer to skip your DataFn server entirely and sync via iCloud?


    Swap `.datafnServer(...)` for `.iCloud(DatafnCloudKitConfiguration(...))` — same client API, CloudKit private database as the backend.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## 4. Query and mutate

You read and write data through three primitives: **mutations** that write, **queries** that read once, and **reactive observers** that auto-update as data changes. All three run against local storage first and reconcile with the server in the background, so your UI stays responsive even on a flaky network.

<Tabs items={["TypeScript", "Swift"]}>
  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    On the web client, every operation is reached through `client.table("<name>")`:

    ```typescript
    // Write — insert a new task
    await client.table("tasks").mutate({
      operation: "insert",
      record: { title: "Ship v1", completed: false, priority: 1 },
    });

    // Read once — fetch incomplete tasks, highest priority first
    const result = await client.table("tasks").query({
      filters: { completed: { $eq: false } },
      sort: ["priority:asc", "id:asc"],
      limit: 20,
    });

    // Subscribe — get a live value that re-emits whenever matching rows change,
    // whether the change came from this device, another tab, or another user.
    const signal = client.table("tasks").signal({
      filters: { completed: { $eq: false } },
    });

    signal.subscribe((value) => {
      console.log("Active tasks:", value);
    });
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab value="Swift">
    On Apple platforms, you read through `DatafnRuntimeObservationSource` and observe reactively with `DatafnObservedQuery` (an `@Observable @MainActor` class — drop it straight into a SwiftUI view):

    ```swift
    import SwiftUI
    import DatafnAppleRuntime

    let source = await runtime.makeObservationSource()

    // Read once
    let tasks = try source.listRecords(resource: "tasks")

    // Reactive observer — re-loads automatically when "tasks" changes
    @MainActor
    struct TaskListView: View {
      let source: DatafnRuntimeObservationSource

      @State private var query = DatafnObservedQuery<[DatafnJSONObject]>(
        resource: "tasks",
        source: source
      )

      var body: some View {
        List(query.value, id: \.self) { row in
          Text(String(describing: row["title"] ?? ""))
        }
      }
    }
    ```

    Mutations from native Swift today flow through the WebView bridge — call `runtime.makeBridgeHost(handlerName:)` to get a `DatafnWKWebViewBridgeHost` and dispatch mutations from your JavaScript layer. A first-class native `mutate()` API is on the roadmap; see [Native Setup](/docs/documentation/client/setup) for the current bridge pattern.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## 5. Use capabilities

The capabilities you declared in step 2 unlock extra operations on the matching tables. Because `trash` was enabled globally every resource can be soft-deleted, and because `archivable` was enabled on `tasks` they can also be archived.

<Tabs items={["TypeScript", "Swift"]}>
  <Tab value="TypeScript">
    Each enabled capability adds methods directly on the table handle:

    ```typescript
    // Soft-delete (from the "trash" capability) — row is hidden but recoverable
    await client.table("tasks").trash("tsk:1");
    await client.table("tasks").restore("tsk:1");

    // Archive (from the "archivable" capability on tasks) — keep around but out of view
    await client.table("tasks").archive("tsk:1");
    await client.table("tasks").unarchive("tsk:1");

    // Queries skip archived and trashed rows by default. Opt them back in explicitly:
    await client.table("tasks").query({
      metadata: { includeArchived: true, includeTrashed: true },
    });
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab value="Swift">
    On Apple, the runtime already understands every capability you declared in your schema — it injects the same system fields (`trashedAt`, `archivedAt`, `createdAt`, etc.) into the local CoreData store, and observers respect them automatically. Today, capability operations themselves (`trash`, `restore`, `archive`, `unarchive`) are issued through the WebView bridge alongside other mutations:

    ```swift
    // Reads honor capabilities out of the box — trashed/archived rows are
    // already hidden from listRecords without any extra flags.
    let activeTasks = try source.listRecords(resource: "tasks")
    ```

    Native Swift convenience methods for capability operations (e.g. `runtime.table("tasks").trash(...)`) are on the roadmap. Track progress in [Capabilities](/docs/documentation/capabilities).
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Capabilities keep boilerplate (timestamps, soft-delete, audit trails, sharing) out of your application code. See [Capabilities](/docs/documentation/capabilities) for the full list.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### DataFn

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs
Description: Self-hosted data management platform with offline-first storage, reactive signals, and a declarative query language.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DataFn is a full-stack data framework for building modern software applications. It provides a unified approach to defining schemas, querying data, managing mutations, and synchronizing state between client and server.

You define a schema. You get back a server, a client, a sync engine, optimistic UI primitives, multi-tenancy, sharing, search hooks, and a native Apple runtime — all with the same DFQL query shape across every layer. It replaces your ORM, query client, sync layer, and realtime stack with one type-safe, offline-first data platform you actually own.


Pick the entry point that matches what you're doing:

- **New to DataFn?** Start with the [Quickstart for your framework](/docs/quickstart).
- **Evaluating?** Read the [Comparison](/docs/comparison) and the [Architecture](/docs/documentation).
- **Building something specific?** Browse the [Recipes](/docs/recipes).
- **Looking up a config or error?** Jump to the [Reference](/docs/reference/routes).

## Batteries included

- Typed query language — DFQL
- Offline-first sync engine
- Reactive signals
- Multi-tenancy with namespace isolation
- Field-level authz
- Per-record sharing
- Auto REST API
- Native Apple runtime (CoreData + CloudKit)

## System Architecture

DataFn connects your client application to your server through DFQL, a structured query language. The client operates offline-first with local storage, syncing changes when online.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Web ["Web Client (Browser)"]
        DC[DatafnClient]
        SIG[Signals]
        STR["Storage — IndexedDB / Memory"]
        SV[Svelte Adapter]
    end

    subgraph Apple ["Native Client (iOS / macOS)"]
        AR[DatafnAppleRuntime]
        SUI[SwiftUI Bindings]
        CDS[CoreData Store]
        CK[CloudKit Sync]
    end

    subgraph Protocol ["DFQL Protocol"]
        Q[Queries]
        M[Mutations]
        T[Transactions]
        LIVE["Live — WebSocket Cursors"]
    end

    subgraph Server ["Server (Node.js / Python)"]
        DS[DatafnServer]
        RT["Routes — DFQL / REST"]
        AUTH["Authorization — Namespaces, Sharing, Capabilities"]
        SE[Sync Engine]
        SEQ["Sequence Store — Redis / KV / DB"]
        WSB[WebSocket Broadcaster]
        PL[Plugins & Search Providers]
    end

    subgraph DB ["Database"]
        AD["Adapters — Drizzle / SQLAlchemy"]
        PG[(PostgreSQL / SQLite)]
    end

    DC --> SIG
    SIG --> SV
    DC --> STR
    DC <-->|"clone / pull / push"| SE
    DC <-->|"query / mutate / transact"| RT
    DC <-.->|live| WSB

    AR --> SUI
    AR --> CDS
    AR <--> CK
    AR <-->|"clone / pull / push"| SE
    AR <-->|"query / mutate / transact"| RT
    AR <-.->|live| WSB

    RT --> AUTH
    RT --> DS
    RT --> PL
    DS --> AD
    SE --> SEQ
    SE --> AD
    AD --> PG
```

Select a section from the sidebar to get started.

Part of [Super functions](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions) and built with care at [21n](https://21n.co).

Description: Pick your stack and ship a working DataFn integration in 10 minutes.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Every quickstart below ends with a working server + client, a single resource, and a reactive query. They're sized for a 10-minute first impression, not for production. For the production-shaped configuration see [Server Setup](/docs/documentation/server/setup) and [Production / Deploy](/docs/documentation/deploy).

## Don't see your stack?

If your backend can speak HTTP, DataFn works. The TypeScript routes are just async functions returning a JSON envelope; you can wire them into any router (Fastify, Koa, h3, AWS Lambda, Vercel, Cloudflare Workers). See [Routes](/docs/reference/routes) for the raw contract.

For client frameworks (React, Vue, Solid), wrap a `createDatafnClient(...)` in your usual state library — `client.table("tasks").signal(...)` returns a subscribable value that fits any reactive system.

### Recipes

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes
Description: Production-tested patterns for shipping with DataFn. Each recipe is self-contained: the schema, the server config, and the client glue.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Recipes are working patterns, not exhaustive guides. Read them when you're about to ship a feature and you want a reference shape for it.

## App patterns

| Recipe | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| [Todo app](/docs/recipes/todo-app) | The minimum viable end-to-end: schema, server, client, optimistic UI. |
| [Kanban board](/docs/recipes/kanban-board) | Ordered lists, drag-and-drop with `position` fields, atomic moves via `transact`. |
| [Chat app](/docs/recipes/chat-app) | Append-only resources, cursor pagination, WebSocket live updates. |
| [Document collab](/docs/recipes/document-collab) | Per-document presence and conflict-free edit semantics. |

## Architecture patterns

| Recipe | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| [Multi-tenant SaaS](/docs/recipes/multi-tenant-saas) | Namespace per tenant; deriving namespaces from auth. |
| [Sharing flows](/docs/recipes/sharing-flows) | Invite-by-email, link-share, share-with-role with the `shareable` capability. |
| [Presence and cursors](/docs/recipes/presence-cursors) | Ephemeral state alongside persisted state. |
| [Offline conflict resolution](/docs/recipes/offline-conflicts) | LWW, version guards, and merge policies. |
| [Optimistic UI](/docs/recipes/optimistic-ui) | Snappy mutations with deterministic rollback. |
| [List virtualization](/docs/recipes/virtualization) | Subscriptions over windowed slices. |
| [Encryption at rest](/docs/recipes/encryption-at-rest) | Field-level encryption via plugins. |
| [Audit logging](/docs/recipes/audit-logging) | Capability-driven audit + outbound logging. |
| [Testing patterns](/docs/recipes/testing) | Deterministic sync, fixture seeding, mock clients. |

## Integration patterns

| Recipe | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| [AuthFn integration](/docs/recipes/authfn-integration) | Sessions → namespaces, role checks in `authorize`. |
| [FileFn integration](/docs/recipes/filefn-integration) | Attaching files to DataFn records. |
| [SearchFn integration](/docs/recipes/searchfn-integration) | Cross-resource search via the `SearchProvider` interface. |

## How to use a recipe

1. Read the recipe end to end before copying.
2. Adapt the schema to your domain. Capabilities (`timestamps`, `audit`, `trash`, etc.) are the levers; pick the ones you need.
3. Mount the routes on the framework you actually use. The recipes lean on Hono in examples, but the pattern is the same for any framework — see the [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart) section.
4. Steal whatever you need from the client glue, then delete the rest.

### API Reference

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/reference
Description: Complete API reference for all DataFn packages.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Packages

DataFn is organized into three packages:

### @datafn/core

Shared types, schema validation, filter evaluation, normalization utilities, date conversion, KV helpers, and plugin hook execution. Used by both client and server.

- [Core Types](/docs/reference/core/types) -- all type definitions
- [Schema Utilities](/docs/reference/core/schema) -- validation and indexing
- [Filter Utilities](/docs/reference/core/filters) -- filter evaluation and operators
- [Normalization](/docs/reference/core/normalize) -- DFQL normalization for caching
- [Date Utilities](/docs/reference/core/date) -- date format conversion
- [KV Utilities](/docs/reference/core/kv) -- built-in key-value resource
- [Hook Utilities](/docs/reference/core/hooks) -- plugin hook execution
- [Error Types](/docs/reference/core/errors) -- error codes and envelopes

### @datafn/client

Browser and Node.js client with offline support, sync engine, reactive signals, event bus, and storage adapters.

- [Client Configuration](/docs/reference/client/config) -- `createDatafnClient` options
- [Query Execution](/docs/reference/client/query) -- client query internals
- [Mutation Execution](/docs/reference/client/mutation) -- client mutation internals
- [Signal API](/docs/reference/client/signal) -- reactive signal system
- [Storage Adapter](/docs/reference/client/storage) -- storage interface
- [Sync Engine](/docs/reference/client/sync) -- sync engine internals
- [Event Bus](/docs/reference/client/events) -- event system
- [Transport](/docs/reference/client/transport) -- HTTP transport and remote adapter

### @datafn/server

Node.js server with route handlers, execution engine, middleware, and WebSocket support.

- [Server Configuration](/docs/reference/server/config) -- `createDatafnServer` options
- [Route Handlers](/docs/reference/server/routes) -- handler internals
- [Middleware](/docs/reference/server/middleware) -- rate limiting and timing
- [Execution Engine](/docs/reference/server/execution) -- query and mutation execution
- [WebSocket Manager](/docs/reference/server/websocket) -- real-time push

## Cli

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### CI Integration

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli/ci-integration
Description: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and CircleCI recipes for DataFn schema validation and migration.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The CLI is designed for CI environments. Every command exits non-zero on failure, supports `--format json`, and reads credentials from env vars rather than disk.

## What to gate in CI

1. **Schema validity** — `datafn validate` on every PR. Catches malformed schemas before they get merged.
2. **Breaking diff detection** — `datafn schema-diff --fail-on breaking` on every PR. Forces explicit review of breaking changes.
3. **Type codegen freshness** — `datafn type-codegen --check` on every PR. Ensures generated types are in sync with the schema.
4. **Migration application** — `datafn schema-migrate apply` on merge. Promotes schema changes to the corresponding environment.

## GitHub Actions

```yaml
# .github/workflows/datafn-ci.yml
name: DataFn CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Validate schema
        run: npx datafn validate
      - name: Schema diff vs main
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        run: |
          npx datafn schema-diff \
            --before "git:${{ github.base_ref }}:schema.datafn.ts" \
            --fail-on breaking \
            --format markdown > /tmp/diff.md
          cat /tmp/diff.md >> $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
      - name: Type codegen freshness
        run: npx datafn type-codegen --check

  apply-staging:
    needs: validate
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Apply pending migrations
        env:
          DATAFN_STAGING_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DATAFN_STAGING_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          for f in migrations/*.ts; do
            npx datafn schema-migrate apply --profile staging --plan "$f"
          done

  apply-production:
    needs: apply-staging
    if: github.event.release.tag_name
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Apply pending migrations
        env:
          DATAFN_PRODUCTION_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DATAFN_PRODUCTION_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          for f in migrations/*.ts; do
            npx datafn schema-migrate apply --profile production --plan "$f"
          done
```

The `environment:` keys gate production with the standard GitHub deployment protection rules — required reviewers, wait timer, etc.

## GitLab CI

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [validate, deploy-staging, deploy-production]

validate:
  stage: validate
  image: node:20
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npx datafn validate
    - >
      if [ -n "$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME" ]; then
        npx datafn schema-diff \
          --before "git:origin/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME:schema.datafn.ts" \
          --fail-on breaking
      fi
    - npx datafn type-codegen --check

deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy-staging
  image: node:20
  only: [main]
  environment: staging
  script:
    - npm ci
    - for f in migrations/*.ts; do npx datafn schema-migrate apply --profile staging --plan "$f"; done

deploy-production:
  stage: deploy-production
  image: node:20
  only: [tags]
  environment: production
  when: manual
  script:
    - npm ci
    - for f in migrations/*.ts; do npx datafn schema-migrate apply --profile production --plan "$f"; done
```

## CircleCI

```yaml
# .circleci/config.yml
version: 2.1

jobs:
  validate:
    docker: [{ image: cimg/node:20.0 }]
    steps:
      - checkout
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx datafn validate
      - run: npx datafn type-codegen --check
      - run:
          name: Schema diff vs main
          command: |
            BASE=${CIRCLE_PR_BASE_BRANCH:-main}
            git fetch origin $BASE
            npx datafn schema-diff \
              --before "git:origin/$BASE:schema.datafn.ts" \
              --fail-on breaking

  apply-staging:
    docker: [{ image: cimg/node:20.0 }]
    steps:
      - checkout
      - run: npm ci
      - run:
          name: Apply migrations
          command: |
            for f in migrations/*.ts; do
              npx datafn schema-migrate apply --profile staging --plan "$f"
            done

workflows:
  ci:
    jobs:
      - validate
      - apply-staging:
          requires: [validate]
          filters: { branches: { only: main } }
```

## OIDC-based auth (GitHub Actions example)

Instead of long-lived bearer tokens, use OIDC token exchange:

```yaml
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
    with: { node-version: 20 }
  - run: npm ci
  - name: Exchange OIDC for DataFn token
    id: token
    run: |
      OIDC_TOKEN=$(curl -sLS \
        -H "Authorization: bearer $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN" \
        "$ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=datafn-prod")
      DATAFN_TOKEN=$(curl -sX POST https://api.example.com/datafn/auth/oidc-exchange \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d "{\"token\":\"$OIDC_TOKEN\"}" | jq -r .access_token)
      echo "DATAFN_TOKEN=$DATAFN_TOKEN" >> $GITHUB_ENV
  - run: |
      for f in migrations/*.ts; do
        npx datafn schema-migrate apply --profile production --plan "$f"
      done
    env:
      DATAFN_PRODUCTION_TOKEN: ${{ env.DATAFN_TOKEN }}
```

OIDC is the recommended pattern for production deploys — no secrets in repo settings, short-lived credentials, audit trail through your IdP.

## Reading the diff in PR comments

The CLI's `--format markdown` output is designed for posting:

```yaml
- name: Post schema diff
  if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
  run: |
    npx datafn schema-diff \
      --before "git:${{ github.base_ref }}:schema.datafn.ts" \
      --format markdown > /tmp/diff.md
- uses: marocchino/sticky-pull-request-comment@v2
  with:
    header: schema-diff
    path: /tmp/diff.md
```

`sticky-pull-request-comment` updates the same comment instead of posting fresh ones — keeps the PR clean.

## See also

- [Environment profiles](/docs/cli/env-profiles)
- [Multi-environment workflows](/docs/cli/multi-env)
- [`datafn schema-diff`](/docs/cli/schema-diff)
- [`datafn schema-migrate`](/docs/cli/schema-migrate)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Drizzle Schema Generation

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli/drizzle-codegen
Description: Generate Drizzle ORM table definitions from your schema.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Overview

The `generateDrizzleSchema(schema, dialect)` function produces a complete Drizzle ORM schema file from a DataFn schema. It validates the schema, ensures the built-in `kv` and [`datafnTimezoneChange`](/docs/dfql/temporal#timezone-change-registry) resources exist, and generates table definitions with column types, indices, foreign keys, and join tables.

```typescript
import { generateDrizzleSchema } from "@datafn/cli";

const code = generateDrizzleSchema(mySchema, "postgres");
// Write `code` to a .ts file
```

## Dialect Support

| Dialect | Table Constructor | Import Path |
|---|---|---|
| `postgres` | `pgTable` | `drizzle-orm/pg-core` |
| `mysql` | `mysqlTable` | `drizzle-orm/mysql-core` |
| `sqlite` | `sqliteTable` | `drizzle-orm/sqlite-core` |

## Column Type Mapping

| Schema Type | PostgreSQL | MySQL | SQLite |
|---|---|---|---|
| `string` | `text()` | `text()` | `text()` |
| `number` | `numeric()` | `int()` | `integer()` |
| `boolean` | `boolean()` | `boolean()` | `integer()` |
| `date` | `bigint({ mode: "number" })` | `bigint({ mode: "number" })` | `integer()` |
| `json` | `jsonb()` | `json()` | `text()` |
| `object` | `jsonb()` | `json()` | `text()` |
| `array` | `jsonb()` | `json()` | `text()` |
| `file` | `text()` | `text()` | `text()` |

## Namespace Column

When `schema.namespaced` is `true` (the default), every table includes an `__ns` column for namespace isolation:

```typescript
export const todos = pgTable("todos", {
  __ns: text("__ns").notNull(),
  completed: boolean("completed").notNull(),
  id: text("id").primaryKey(),
  title: text("title").notNull(),
}, (table) => [
  index("idx_todos___ns").on(table.__ns),
]);
```

Set `namespaced: false` in your schema to omit the `__ns` column.

## Index Generation

Each table may include:

- **Namespace index** -- `idx_{table}___ns` when namespace isolation is enabled.
- **Base indices** -- one index per field listed in `indices.base`.
