- **Relation FK indices** -- `{table}_{fk_column}_rel_idx` for each generated foreign-key column (see below). Htree relations also index the path column.
- **Join table unique index** -- `{joinTable}_{from}_{to}_idx` for many-many relations.
- **Join table directional indices** -- `{joinTable}_{from}_idx` and `{joinTable}_{to}_idx` for efficient traversal in either direction.

## Join Tables

For `many-many` relations, a join table is generated with:

- The `from` and `to` columns (default names: `from` and `to`, overridable via `joinColumns`).
- An `id` column as the primary key.
- Any `metadata` fields from the relation schema.
- A unique index on `(from, to)`.
- Directional indices on `from` and on `to`.

The join table name defaults to `__datafn_join_{from}_{relation}` unless `joinTable` is specified.

For [polymorphic](/docs/dfql/schema/relations#polymorphic-relations) many-many relations (array `from`/`to`), the join table also gets `fromResource` / `toResource` discriminator columns, and the unique and directional indices include them:

```typescript
fromResource: text("from_resource").notNull(),
toResource: text("to_resource").notNull(),
// uniqueIndex("resource_items_from_to_idx").on(fromResource, from, toResource, to)
// index("resource_items_from_idx").on(fromResource, from)
// index("resource_items_to_idx").on(toResource, to)
```

## Relation Foreign Keys

When a relation (or the schema) uses [`integrity: "database"`](/docs/dfql/schema/relations#relation-integrity), codegen emits real foreign-key columns, indices, and constraints for FK-backed relations (`many-one`, `one-many`, `htree`). The FK column is generated on the holding resource if it is not already declared:

| Relation type | Default FK column | Extra columns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `many-one` | `fkField` or `{relation}Id` | `{relation}Resource` when `to` is polymorphic |
| `one-many` | `fkField` or `inverse` or `{from}Id` | `{...}Resource` when `from` is polymorphic |
| `htree` | `fkField` or `inverse` or `parentId` | `pathField` (default `parentPath`); `{parent}Resource` when polymorphic |

`onDelete` policies map to Drizzle `ON DELETE` actions on resource foreign keys:

| `onDelete` policy | Drizzle action |
| --- | --- |
| `cascade` | `.onDelete("cascade")` |
| `restrict` | `.onDelete("restrict")` |
| `setNull` / `detach` | `.onDelete("set null")` |
| _(absent)_ | no `.onDelete` clause |

Example (namespaced, `onDelete: { to: "setNull" }`):

```typescript
index("task_project_id_rel_idx").on(table.__ns, table.projectId),
foreignKey({
  columns: [table.__ns, table.projectId],
  foreignColumns: [project.__ns, project.id],
}).onDelete("set null"),
```

Foreign-key **constraints** are not emitted for polymorphic join tables (which use discriminator columns instead). Join-table FKs are emitted only when integrity is `"database"` and the endpoint is non-polymorphic; their `onDelete` mapping is `restrict` → `restrict`, and `cascade`/`detach`/`setNull` → `cascade`.

## Built-in Resources

Generated schemas always include the internal `__datafn_*` tables, the built-in `kv` table, and the [`datafnTimezoneChange`](/docs/dfql/temporal#timezone-change-registry) table (injected via `ensureBuiltinTemporal`). The temporal table's `number` columns mean minimal Postgres schemas now also import `numeric`.

## Example Output

```typescript
// Generated by @datafn/cli. DO NOT EDIT.
// Database: postgres
import { boolean, index, pgTable, text } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";

export const todos = pgTable("todos", {
  __ns: text("__ns").notNull(),
  completed: boolean("completed").notNull(),
  id: text("id").primaryKey(),
  title: text("title").notNull(),
}, (table) => [
  index("idx_todos___ns").on(table.__ns),
]);

export const schema = { todos };
```

## Exports

All tables are exported as named constants. A `schema` object is exported that maps table variable names to their definitions, sorted alphabetically.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Environment Profiles

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli/env-profiles
Description: Manage dev, staging, and production configuration with the CLI.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The CLI honors environment profiles for any command that connects to a running DataFn server. Profiles are TOML/JSON files in `.datafn/profiles/` that specify the server URL, auth, namespace, and schema hash to use.

This lets you run `datafn schema-migrate apply` against staging vs production without retyping connection details.

## Profile file format

`.datafn/profiles/staging.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "staging",
  "server": {
    "baseUrl": "https://staging.example.com/datafn",
    "websocketUrl": "wss://staging.example.com/datafn/ws"
  },
  "auth": {
    "kind": "bearer",
    "tokenEnvVar": "DATAFN_STAGING_TOKEN"
  },
  "namespace": "team:staging",
  "schemaHash": "auto"
}
```

`.datafn/profiles/production.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "production",
  "server": {
    "baseUrl": "https://api.example.com/datafn",
    "websocketUrl": "wss://api.example.com/datafn/ws"
  },
  "auth": {
    "kind": "bearer",
    "tokenEnvVar": "DATAFN_PRODUCTION_TOKEN"
  },
  "namespace": "team:production",
  "schemaHash": "manual"
}
```

## Selecting a profile

```bash
# Via flag
datafn schema-migrate apply --profile staging --plan migrations/2026-05-21.ts

# Via env var
DATAFN_PROFILE=production datafn schema-migrate apply --plan migrations/2026-05-21.ts
```

If neither is set, the CLI looks for `.datafn/profiles/default.json`.

## Schema-hash modes

The `schemaHash` field controls how the CLI handles the schema hash:

- `"auto"` (default): The CLI reads the hash from the server's `/datafn/meta` endpoint and uses it. Safe for dev/staging.
- `"manual"`: The CLI requires `--schema-hash <value>` on the command line. Safest for production — prevents accidentally running a migration against the wrong schema version.
- `"<explicit hash>"`: The CLI verifies the server's hash matches this string before proceeding.

## Auth options

```json
{ "auth": { "kind": "bearer", "tokenEnvVar": "DATAFN_TOKEN" } }
{ "auth": { "kind": "bearer", "token": "literal-token" } }    // Discouraged
{ "auth": { "kind": "oauth", "clientId": "...", "audience": "..." } }
{ "auth": { "kind": "command", "command": "aws sso login --output json" } }
```

The `command` kind shells out and reads `Authorization` from stdout — useful for short-lived AWS / Vault / Doppler credentials.

## Listing profiles

```bash
datafn profiles list
```

```
NAME         BASE URL                                NAMESPACE        SCHEMA HASH
default      http://localhost:3000/datafn            local            auto
staging      https://staging.example.com/datafn      team:staging     auto
production   https://api.example.com/datafn          team:production  manual
```

## Adding a profile interactively

```bash
datafn profiles add my-profile
```

Prompts for base URL, namespace, auth, and writes the file. Non-interactive form:

```bash
datafn profiles add my-profile \
  --base-url https://api.example.com/datafn \
  --namespace team:production \
  --auth-bearer-env DATAFN_TOKEN \
  --schema-hash-mode manual
```

## Secrets policy

- The CLI **never** writes tokens to disk. Always reference an env var.
- `tokenEnvVar` is resolved from the shell environment at execution time.
- For machine-to-machine in CI, use OIDC where possible (`auth.kind = "oauth"` with a token exchange).

## Profile composition

For settings shared across profiles, use `extends`:

```json
{
  "name": "production-eu",
  "extends": "production",
  "server": { "baseUrl": "https://eu.example.com/datafn" }
}
```

The CLI merges parent → child, with child winning.

## See also

- [Multi-environment workflows](/docs/cli/multi-env)
- [CI integration](/docs/cli/ci-integration)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Generate

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli/generate
Description: Generate TypeScript types and database schemas from your DataFn schema.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Usage

```bash
datafn generate [flags]
```

The `generate` command reads your DataFn schema and produces TypeScript type definitions and ORM-specific database schema files.

## Flags

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--schema` | `string` | auto-discovered | Path to schema file. |
| `--adapter` | `drizzle` | -- | Required. ORM adapter for schema generation. |
| `--database` | `postgres \| mysql \| sqlite` | -- | Required. Target database dialect. |
| `--output` | `string` | `./` | Output directory for generated files. |

## What Gets Generated

Running `datafn generate` produces two outputs:

1. **TypeScript type definitions** -- interfaces for each resource, a `Tables` mapping type, and a `TypedClient` type for type-safe client code.
2. **ORM schema file** -- table definitions for your chosen adapter and database dialect (e.g., Drizzle `pgTable` definitions for PostgreSQL).

## Example

```bash
# Generate Drizzle schema for PostgreSQL
datafn generate --adapter drizzle --database postgres --output ./src/generated

# Generate from a specific schema file
datafn generate --adapter drizzle --database postgres --schema ./config/schema.datafn.ts --output ./src/db

# Generate for SQLite
datafn generate --adapter drizzle --database sqlite --output ./src/generated
```

Given this schema:

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export default defineSchema({
  resources: [
    {
      name: "todos",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "td",
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "completed", type: "boolean", required: true },
        { name: "dueDate", type: "date", required: false },
      ],
    },
  ],
});
```

The command generates a TypeScript file with:

```typescript
import type { DatafnClient, DatafnTable } from "@datafn/client";

export interface Todos {
  completed: boolean;
  dueDate?: number;
  title: string;
}

export interface Tables {
  todos: Todos;
}

export type TypedClient = DatafnClient & {
  todos: DatafnTable<Todos>;
};
```

And a Drizzle schema file with table definitions matching your resources and dialect. See [Type Generation](/docs/cli/type-codegen) and [Drizzle Schema Generation](/docs/cli/drizzle-codegen) for details on each output.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Multi-Environment Workflows

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli/multi-env
Description: Promote schemas and migrations across dev → staging → production safely.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A typical DataFn deployment has three or more environments: local dev, staging, production. The CLI is built around the assumption that you'll iterate locally, validate in staging, then promote to production with the same artifacts.

## The promotion pattern

```
local dev          staging              production
└── apply ◄──────┐ └── apply ◄────────┐ └── apply
    immediate    │     after PR       │     after release
                 │                    │
              same migration file, same schema hash
```

The unit of promotion is a **migration file**. The same file, byte-for-byte, runs against all three environments. The CLI verifies the schema hash chain on each environment to prevent drift.

## End-to-end flow

### 1. Edit the schema locally

```typescript
// schema.datafn.ts
export default defineSchema({
  resources: [
    { name: "tasks", version: 1, fields: [...] },
    // New:
    { name: "projects", version: 1, fields: [...] },
  ],
});
```

### 2. Diff against main

```bash
datafn schema-diff --before main:schema.datafn.ts
```

```
+ Resource: projects (safe)
```

### 3. Generate a migration (if needed)

For additive changes (new resource, new optional field), you don't need a migration — the runtime handles them at startup.

For breaking or risky changes, generate one:

```bash
datafn schema-migrate generate \
  --before main:schema.datafn.ts \
  --out migrations/
```

### 4. Apply to local dev

```bash
datafn schema-migrate apply \
  --profile default \
  --plan migrations/2026-05-21-add-projects.ts
```

### 5. Open a PR

The PR includes:

- The updated `schema.datafn.ts`
- The migration file (if any)
- Any code changes that depend on the schema

CI runs `datafn schema-diff --fail-on breaking` to flag unsafe changes. See [CI integration](/docs/cli/ci-integration).

### 6. Merge → CD deploys to staging

A deploy step in CI runs:

```bash
datafn schema-migrate apply \
  --profile staging \
  --plan migrations/2026-05-21-add-projects.ts
```

The CLI verifies staging's current schema hash matches `schemaHashBefore` and applies the migration. If staging is behind (e.g. a prior migration wasn't applied), the CLI lists pending migrations and fails until the chain is consistent.

### 7. Smoke test in staging

Manual or automated. Confirm the app runs against the new schema before promoting.

### 8. Promote to production

```bash
datafn schema-migrate apply \
  --profile production \
  --schema-hash <expected> \
  --plan migrations/2026-05-21-add-projects.ts
```

Use `--schema-hash` to assert the production state explicitly — defense against running the wrong migration against production.

## Drift detection

If staging and production schema hashes diverge, the CLI flags it:

```bash
datafn schema-migrate status --profile staging --profile production
```

```
ENV         CURRENT HASH    LAST MIGRATION                              PENDING
staging     def456          2026-05-21-add-projects                     0
production  abc123          2026-05-15-rename-title                     1
            └─ Pending: migrations/2026-05-21-add-projects.ts
```

Production is behind staging by one migration. The promotion command applies it.

## Rollback strategy

Production rollback is the same migration file's `down`:

```bash
datafn schema-migrate rollback \
  --profile production \
  --plan migrations/2026-05-21-add-projects.ts \
  --schema-hash <expected-after-hash>
```

The CLI verifies the schema hash matches `schemaHashAfter`, then applies `down` to bring it back to `schemaHashBefore`.

For non-reversible migrations (data loss, type narrowing), `down` should throw with a clear message. The team knows ahead of time that rolling forward (a new migration) is the only safe path.

## Multi-region production

For deployments spanning multiple regions:

```bash
for region in eu us asia; do
  datafn schema-migrate apply \
    --profile production-$region \
    --plan migrations/2026-05-21-add-projects.ts
done
```

Migrations are idempotent — running the same plan across regions does the right thing.

## Per-namespace migrations

If your store has multiple namespaces (multi-tenant SaaS), you may want to roll out a migration to one tenant first:

```bash
datafn schema-migrate apply \
  --profile production \
  --namespace org:beta-tester \
  --plan migrations/2026-05-21-add-projects.ts
```

Then expand:

```bash
datafn schema-migrate apply \
  --profile production \
  --plan migrations/2026-05-21-add-projects.ts
# Default: all namespaces
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Don't edit applied migrations.** Once a migration has been applied in any environment, its file is locked. Editing it after the fact breaks reproducibility — the same hash chain no longer corresponds to the same data transformation. Create a new migration instead.
- **Don't skip staging.** The whole point of staging is to find migration problems before production. The CLI's hash chain assumes a linear progression.
- **Don't run migrations as part of the app boot.** App boot should be idempotent and fast; migrations should be explicit, separate, and gated.

## See also

- [`datafn schema-migrate`](/docs/cli/schema-migrate)
- [Environment profiles](/docs/cli/env-profiles)
- [CI integration](/docs/cli/ci-integration)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### datafn schema-diff

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli/schema-diff
Description: Compare two schema versions and produce a structured diff.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

`datafn schema-diff` compares two schema files (or a file vs a recorded version) and reports the changes in a structured form. Use it in CI to enforce migration safety policies before merging.

## Usage

```bash
datafn schema-diff --before <path> --after <path>
```

| Flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--before` | — | Older schema (file, JSON, or `git:<ref>:<path>`) |
| `--after` | discovered | Newer schema (defaults to discovered schema) |
| `--format` | `text` | `text`, `json`, or `markdown` |
| `--fail-on` | `none` | Exit non-zero if diff contains changes of severity `breaking`, `risky`, or `any` |

Examples:

```bash
# Diff working copy against last tagged release
datafn schema-diff --before git:v1.2.0:schema.datafn.ts

# Machine-readable for CI
datafn schema-diff --before main:schema.datafn.ts --format json > diff.json

# Fail merge if breaking changes
datafn schema-diff --before main:schema.datafn.ts --fail-on breaking
```

## Diff categories

Each change is categorized by severity:

| Severity | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| `safe` | New resource added, new optional field added, new index, capability flipped on with backfill |
| `risky` | Field type widened, capability flipped off, relation cardinality changed in compatible direction |
| `breaking` | Field removed, field type narrowed (string → int), required field added with no default, namespace strategy changed |

The `breaking` set is what blocks safe deployment.

## Output format

### Text (default)

```
+ Resource: comments
+   field: parentCommentId (string, optional)
~ Resource: tasks
~   field: priority changed: int → "low" | "medium" | "high" (breaking)
~   capability: archivable added (safe)
- Resource: legacyAttachments (breaking)
```

### JSON

```json
{
  "resources": {
    "added": ["comments"],
    "removed": ["legacyAttachments"],
    "changed": {
      "tasks": {
        "fields": {
          "changed": {
            "priority": { "before": "int", "after": "string", "severity": "breaking" }
          }
        },
        "capabilities": {
          "added": ["archivable"]
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "severity": "breaking"
}
```

### Markdown

GitHub-flavoured table suitable for posting to PR comments. The CLI `--format markdown` output is what `datafn-action` posts.

## Integration with PR review

A common pattern:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/schema-diff.yml
on: pull_request

jobs:
  schema-diff:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - run: npm ci
      - run: |
          npx datafn schema-diff \
            --before "git:${{ github.base_ref }}:schema.datafn.ts" \
            --format markdown > /tmp/diff.md
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const fs = require("node:fs");
            const body = fs.readFileSync("/tmp/diff.md", "utf-8");
            github.rest.issues.createComment({
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              body: "## Schema diff\n\n" + body,
            });
```

This posts a diff comment on every PR. Reviewers see exactly what schema surface changed.

## What it doesn't do

`schema-diff` reports the shape of change; it doesn't generate a migration. For that, see [`datafn schema-migrate`](/docs/cli/schema-migrate). For runtime migration semantics, see [Schema migration](/docs/documentation/sync/schema-migration).

## See also

- [`datafn schema-migrate`](/docs/cli/schema-migrate)
- [CI integration](/docs/cli/ci-integration)
- [Schema migration](/docs/documentation/sync/schema-migration)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### datafn schema-migrate

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli/schema-migrate
Description: Generate and apply schema migration plans.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

`datafn schema-migrate` turns a [schema diff](/docs/cli/schema-diff) into an executable migration plan and applies it to your data store. Use it for the small set of changes that need explicit data transformation (renames, type changes with custom mapping, backfills).

The simpler case — additive changes only — doesn't need a migration. The runtime handles those at startup. Migrations exist for the harder cases.

## Usage

```bash
datafn schema-migrate generate --before <path>
datafn schema-migrate apply --plan migrations/<file>.ts
datafn schema-migrate status
```

## Subcommands

### `generate`

```bash
datafn schema-migrate generate --before main:schema.datafn.ts --out migrations/
```

Reads the diff between `--before` and the current schema, generates a TypeScript migration file with `up` / `down` stubs:

```typescript
// migrations/2026-05-21T12-00-00-rename-priority.ts
import { defineMigration } from "@datafn/migrate";

export default defineMigration({
  id: "2026-05-21T12-00-00-rename-priority",
  description: "Convert priority from int to string enum",
  schemaHashBefore: "abc123",
  schemaHashAfter: "def456",
  resources: ["tasks"],

  up: async ({ stream, batch }) => {
    for await (const task of stream("tasks")) {
      await batch.set("tasks", task.id, {
        priority: ["low", "medium", "high"][task.priority - 1] ?? "medium",
      });
    }
  },

  down: async ({ stream, batch }) => {
    for await (const task of stream("tasks")) {
      await batch.set("tasks", task.id, {
        priority: { low: 1, medium: 2, high: 3 }[task.priority] ?? 2,
      });
    }
  },
});
```

Replace the body with your transformation logic.

### `apply`

```bash
datafn schema-migrate apply --plan migrations/2026-05-21T12-00-00-rename-priority.ts
```

Runs the migration. Behavior:

1. Validates the migration's `schemaHashBefore` matches the store's current hash.
2. Starts a transaction.
3. Streams affected resources and applies `up`.
4. On success, advances the store's schema hash to `schemaHashAfter`.
5. On failure, rolls back and exits non-zero.

Flags:

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--dry-run` | Report what would change without writing |
| `--namespace <ns>` | Apply only to a specific namespace (default: all) |
| `--batch-size <n>` | Tune batch size (default 500) |
| `--checkpoint <path>` | Persist progress for resumable runs |

### `status`

```bash
datafn schema-migrate status
```

Shows the current store schema hash, last applied migration, and pending migrations (files in `migrations/` that haven't been applied).

### `rollback`

```bash
datafn schema-migrate rollback --plan migrations/<file>.ts
```

Runs the `down` function. Reverses `up`. Same flags as `apply`.

## Migration safety rules

The CLI enforces these by default; pass `--force` to override (don't).

1. **Hash match required.** `apply` refuses to run if `schemaHashBefore` doesn't match the store's current hash. Prevents replaying an old migration on a future schema.
2. **One in-flight migration.** Concurrent migrations on the same store fail with `MIGRATION_LOCKED`.
3. **Idempotent re-runs.** If `apply` is re-invoked on the same migration, it's a no-op (the hash already matches `schemaHashAfter`).
4. **Forward-only locks.** Once a migration has been applied in production, the file is locked — modifying it later breaks reproducibility. Convention: create new migrations rather than editing applied ones.

## Where it runs

Migrations run **server-side**, against the authoritative database. Clients re-clone after schema-hash mismatch on their next sync. You don't need a client-side migration.

For the client experience after a server migration, see [Schema migration](/docs/documentation/sync/schema-migration).

## Example: rename a field

Schema before:

```typescript
{ name: "title", type: "string", required: true }
```

Schema after:

```typescript
{ name: "name", type: "string", required: true }
```

Generated migration:

```typescript
import { defineMigration } from "@datafn/migrate";

export default defineMigration({
  id: "2026-05-21-rename-title-to-name",
  description: "Rename tasks.title to tasks.name",
  schemaHashBefore: "abc123",
  schemaHashAfter: "def456",
  resources: ["tasks"],

  up: async ({ stream, batch }) => {
    for await (const task of stream("tasks")) {
      await batch.set("tasks", task.id, { name: task.title });
      // The "title" field is dropped by the schema-hash change.
    }
  },

  down: async ({ stream, batch }) => {
    for await (const task of stream("tasks")) {
      await batch.set("tasks", task.id, { title: task.name });
    }
  },
});
```

## Example: type change with custom map

Already shown above (`priority: int → string enum`). The pattern is: stream, transform, write.

## Example: backfill from another resource

```typescript
up: async ({ stream, batch, get }) => {
  for await (const task of stream("tasks")) {
    const project = await get("projects", task.projectId);
    if (!project) continue;
    await batch.set("tasks", task.id, { projectName: project.name });
  }
}
```

## Performance

Large migrations are streamed in batches. The runtime emits progress events:

```
[migrate] tasks: 12,500/45,000 (28%)
[migrate] tasks: complete in 4m 12s
```

For very large stores, use `--checkpoint <path>` to persist progress; if the migration is interrupted, the next `apply --checkpoint <path>` resumes from where it stopped.

## See also

- [`datafn schema-diff`](/docs/cli/schema-diff)
- [Schema migration runtime](/docs/documentation/sync/schema-migration)
- [Migrations section](/docs/documentation/migrations/overview)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Type Generation

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli/type-codegen
Description: Generate TypeScript interfaces from your schema.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Overview

The `generateTypes(schema)` function produces TypeScript interface definitions from a DataFn schema. The schema is validated before code generation -- invalid schemas are rejected deterministically via envelope.

```typescript
import { generateTypes } from "@datafn/cli";

const code = generateTypes(mySchema);
// Write `code` to a .ts file
```

## Generated Output

For each resource, `generateTypes` produces:

1. **Resource interfaces** -- one interface per resource with typed fields, including [relation-derived foreign-key fields](#relation-derived-fields).
2. **Join table interfaces** -- for `many-many` relations that have `metadata`, `capabilities`, or a [polymorphic](/docs/dfql/schema/relations#polymorphic-relations) `from`/`to` endpoint.
3. **`Tables` type** -- maps resource names (and join table names) to their interfaces.
4. **`TypedClient` type** -- extends `DatafnClient` with typed table accessors.

All output is **deterministic**: resources, fields, and join tables are sorted by name.

## Relation-Derived Fields

`generateTypes` merges relation foreign-key fields into the holding resource's interface, even if you do not declare them in `fields`. They follow the same naming rules as the [Drizzle FK columns](/docs/cli/drizzle-codegen#relation-foreign-keys) (e.g. a `many-one` relation `project` with `fkField: "projectId"` adds `projectId?: string`). Generated FK fields are optional `string`. Fields you declare explicitly always take precedence.

Polymorphic many-many join interfaces additionally include `fromResource: string` and/or `toResource: string` discriminator fields when those endpoints are polymorphic and the field is not already part of `metadata`.

## Field Type Mapping

| Schema Type | TypeScript Type |
|---|---|
| `string` | `string` |
| `number` | `number` |
| `boolean` | `boolean` |
| `date` | `number` |
| `object` | `Record<string, unknown>` |
| `array` | `unknown[]` |
| `file` | `string` |
| `json` | `unknown` |

## Null and Undefined Handling

- Fields with `required: true` are non-optional: `title: string`.
- Fields with `required: false` are optional: `dueDate?: number`.

## Example

Given this schema:

```typescript
const schema = defineSchema({
  resources: [
    {
      name: "tasks",
      version: 1,
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "priority", type: "number", required: false },
        { name: "metadata", type: "json", required: false },
      ],
    },
    {
      name: "users",
      version: 1,
      fields: [
        { name: "email", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "avatar", type: "file", required: false },
      ],
    },
  ],
  relations: [
    {
      from: "tasks",
      to: "users",
      type: "many-many",
      relation: "assignees",
      inverse: "assignedTasks",
      metadata: [
        { name: "role", type: "string" },
      ],
    },
  ],
});
```

The generated TypeScript is:

```typescript
import type { DatafnClient, DatafnTable } from "@datafn/client";

export interface Tasks {
  metadata?: unknown;
  priority?: number;
  title: string;
}

export interface Users {
  avatar?: string;
  email: string;
}

export interface __datafn_join_tasks_assignees {
  fromId: string;
  role: string;
  toId: string;
}

export interface Tables {
  tasks: Tasks;
  users: Users;
  __datafn_join_tasks_assignees: __datafn_join_tasks_assignees;
}

export type TypedClient = DatafnClient & {
  tasks: DatafnTable<Tasks>;
  users: DatafnTable<Users>;
};
```



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Validate

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/cli/validate
Description: Validate your DataFn schema file.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Usage

```bash
datafn validate [--schema <path>]
```

The `validate` command checks your schema file for structural errors and reports them with detailed paths.

## What Gets Validated

The command uses `validateSchema()` from `@datafn/core` internally and checks:

- **Structure** -- `resources` must be a non-empty array of objects. Each resource must have `name` (string), `version` (integer), and `fields` (array).
- **Field types** -- each field must declare a valid `type`: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, `object`, `array`, `file`, or `json`.
- **Uniqueness** -- resource names must be unique across the schema. Field names must be unique within each resource.
- **Relation integrity** -- `from` and `to` in relations must reference declared resource names. `joinTable` must be a string. `joinColumns` must have `from` and `to` string properties.
- **Index validation** -- index field names must match declared fields within each resource.
- **Limits** -- maximum 100 resources, maximum 200 fields per resource.

## Deterministic Rejection via Envelope

Validation returns a `DatafnEnvelope<DatafnSchema>`. On failure, the envelope contains an error with a specific code, message, and path:

```typescript
{
  ok: false,
  error: {
    code: "SCHEMA_INVALID",
    message: "Invalid schema: duplicate field name: title",
    details: { path: "resources" }
  }
}
```

On success, the envelope contains the normalized schema with indices converted to `{ base, search, vector }` form and relations defaulting to an empty array.

## Example

```bash
# Validate using auto-discovered schema
datafn validate

# Validate a specific file
datafn validate --schema ./config/schema.json
```

A valid schema prints a confirmation line (for example, `✓ Schema is valid: /abs/path/schema.datafn.ts`) and exits with code 0. An invalid schema prints the error details and exits with a non-zero code.



================================================================================
## Dfql
================================================================================


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Aggregations

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/aggregations
Description: Compute aggregate values over record sets.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DFQL supports grouped aggregation queries using `groupBy`, `aggregations`, and `having`. These are analogous to SQL `GROUP BY`, aggregate functions, and `HAVING` clauses.

## Supported Operations

| Operation | Description |
|---|---|
| `count` | Total number of records in the group. Not null-filtered -- counts all records regardless of field value. |
| `sum` | Sum of non-null numeric values. |
| `min` | Minimum non-null value. |
| `max` | Maximum non-null value. |
| `avg` | Average of non-null numeric values. |

## Basic Aggregation

An aggregation query requires `groupBy` (an array of field names) and `aggregations` (a map of alias to `{ op, field }`):

```typescript
const query: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "orders",
  version: 1,
  groupBy: ["status"],
  aggregations: {
    totalAmount: { op: "sum", field: "amount" },
    orderCount: { op: "count", field: "id" },
  },
};
// Result: { groups: [
//   { status: "pending", totalAmount: 2500, orderCount: 12 },
//   { status: "shipped", totalAmount: 8400, orderCount: 34 },
// ]}
```

## Multiple Group Keys

Group by multiple fields to create composite groups:

```typescript
{
  resource: "orders",
  version: 1,
  groupBy: ["status", "region"],
  aggregations: {
    total: { op: "sum", field: "amount" },
    avgAmount: { op: "avg", field: "amount" },
  },
}
// Groups: status + region combinations
```

## Null Semantics

Aggregation follows SQL-like null semantics:

- **count**: Returns the total number of records in the group, including those where the specified field is null or undefined. `count` counts records, not values.
- **sum, min, max, avg**: Exclude null and undefined values from the calculation. If all values are null, the result is `null`.
- **Empty groups**: If a group has zero records (which should not happen with groupBy), aggregations return `null`.

```typescript
// Given records: [{ amount: 10 }, { amount: null }, { amount: 20 }]
// count("amount") = 3  (counts records, not non-null values)
// sum("amount")   = 30 (excludes null)
// avg("amount")   = 15 (30 / 2 non-null values)
// min("amount")   = 10
// max("amount")   = 20
```

## Having Clause

Use `having` to filter groups after aggregation. The `having` clause uses the same filter syntax as regular query filters, but operates on the aggregated result rows (group keys and aggregation aliases):

```typescript
{
  resource: "orders",
  version: 1,
  groupBy: ["customerId"],
  aggregations: {
    totalSpent: { op: "sum", field: "amount" },
    orderCount: { op: "count", field: "id" },
  },
  having: {
    totalSpent: { $gte: 1000 },
    orderCount: { $gte: 5 },
  },
}
// Only returns groups where totalSpent >= 1000 AND orderCount >= 5
```

## Combining with Filters

Filters are applied before grouping. Use `filters` to narrow the input records, then `groupBy` and `aggregations` to summarize:

```typescript
{
  resource: "orders",
  version: 1,
  filters: {
    createdAt: { $after: 1700000000000 },
    status: { $ne: "cancelled" },
  },
  groupBy: ["region"],
  aggregations: {
    revenue: { op: "sum", field: "amount" },
    maxOrder: { op: "max", field: "amount" },
  },
  having: {
    revenue: { $gt: 0 },
  },
}
```

## Sorting Aggregated Results

Aggregation results can be sorted by group keys or aggregation aliases:

```typescript
{
  resource: "orders",
  version: 1,
  groupBy: ["region"],
  aggregations: {
    revenue: { op: "sum", field: "amount" },
  },
  sort: ["-revenue"],
}
```

If no `sort` is specified, results are sorted by the group keys in ascending order.

## Pagination

Aggregation results support the same pagination as regular queries. Use `limit`, `offset`, or `cursor` to paginate through grouped results:

```typescript
{
  resource: "orders",
  version: 1,
  groupBy: ["customerId"],
  aggregations: {
    total: { op: "sum", field: "amount" },
  },
  sort: ["-total"],
  limit: 10,
}
```

## Temporal Grouping

In addition to grouping by raw field values, you can group by **calendar periods** (day, week, month, …) in a specific timezone using a [`temporal`](/docs/dfql/temporal) clause with `groupBy`. This is the time-series equivalent of `groupBy`.

```typescript
import { time } from "@datafn/core";

{
  resource: "sessions",
  version: 1,
  temporal: time.groupByDay("startedAt", { alias: "day", timezone: "user" }),
  aggregations: {
    count: { op: "count", field: "*" },
    minutes: { op: "sum", field: "minutes" },
  },
}
// Result groups, keyed by the start of each day in the user's timezone:
// {
//   groups: [
//     { day: "2026-05-17T18:30:00.000Z", count: 2, minutes: 30 },
//     { day: "2026-05-18T18:30:00.000Z", count: 1, minutes: 30 },
//   ]
// }
```

Notes:

- The temporal group **alias** (`day` above) becomes a group key and can be used in `sort` and `having`, exactly like a `groupBy` field.
- When no `sort` is provided, results are ordered by temporal aliases ascending.
- A query with a temporal `groupBy` is routed to aggregate execution even without an explicit `groupBy` array.
- Temporal grouping can be combined with regular `groupBy` fields and `aggregations`.

See [Temporal](/docs/dfql/temporal) for the full clause reference, timezone resolution, and the `time` builder.

## Programmatic Aggregation

The `calculateAggregation` function computes a single aggregation over an array of records:

```typescript
import { calculateAggregation } from "@datafn/core";

const records = [
  { id: "1", amount: 100 },
  { id: "2", amount: null },
  { id: "3", amount: 200 },
];

calculateAggregation("sum", "amount", records);   // 300
calculateAggregation("count", "amount", records);  // 3
calculateAggregation("avg", "amount", records);    // 150
calculateAggregation("min", "amount", records);    // 100
calculateAggregation("max", "amount", records);    // 200
```



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Filters

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/filters
Description: Filter records with comparison, set, string, and logical operators.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Filters are the primary mechanism for narrowing query results. A filter is a JSON object where keys are field names and values describe the conditions records must satisfy.

## Shorthand Syntax

For simple cases, DFQL supports shorthand filter values:

```typescript
// Scalar value becomes $eq
{ completed: false }
// Equivalent to: { completed: { $eq: false } }

// Array value becomes $in
{ status: ["active", "pending"] }
// Equivalent to: { status: { $in: ["active", "pending"] } }
```

## Operator Normalization

Operators can be written with or without the `$` prefix. Non-prefixed operators are automatically remapped:

```typescript
// These are equivalent:
{ priority: { gte: 3 } }
{ priority: { $gte: 3 } }
```

The full remap table:

| Input | Normalized |
|---|---|
| `eq` | `$eq` |
| `ne` | `$ne` |
| `gt` | `$gt` |
| `gte` | `$gte` |
| `lt` | `$lt` |
| `lte` | `$lte` |
| `in` | `$in` |
| `not_in` | `$nin` |
| `like` | `$like` |
| `ilike` | `$ilike` |
| `not_like` | `$not_like` |
| `not_ilike` | `$not_ilike` |
| `is_null` | `$is_null` |
| `is_not_null` | `$is_not_null` |
| `is_empty` | `$is_empty` |
| `is_not_empty` | `$is_not_empty` |
| `before` | `$before` |
| `after` | `$after` |
| `between` | `$between` |
| `not_between` | `$not_between` |

You can normalize filters programmatically:

```typescript
import { normalizeFilterOps } from "@datafn/core";

const normalized = normalizeFilterOps({ priority: { gte: 3 } });
// { priority: { $gte: 3 } }
```

### Undefined Stripping

`normalizeFilterOps` strips `undefined` at every level so optional UI filters can be passed through without affecting results:

```typescript
normalizeFilterOps({
  isArchived: undefined,
  status: { eq: "active", ne: undefined },
  dueAt: undefined,
});
// { status: { $eq: "active" } }
```

Top-level keys whose value is `undefined` are omitted, `undefined` operator values are dropped, and a field operator object that becomes empty after stripping is removed entirely. `null` is preserved (use it with `$is_null` / `$eq` to match null values).

## Comparison Operators

| Operator | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `$eq` | Equal to | `{ status: { $eq: "active" } }` |
| `$ne` | Not equal to | `{ status: { $ne: "archived" } }` |
| `$gt` | Greater than | `{ priority: { $gt: 3 } }` |
| `$gte` | Greater than or equal | `{ priority: { $gte: 3 } }` |
| `$lt` | Less than | `{ priority: { $lt: 5 } }` |
| `$lte` | Less than or equal | `{ priority: { $lte: 5 } }` |

```typescript
{
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  filters: {
    priority: { $gte: 3, $lte: 8 },
  },
}
```

Multiple operators on the same field are ANDed together. The example above matches records where `3 <= priority <= 8`.

## Set Operators

| Operator | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `$in` | Value is in array | `{ status: { $in: ["active", "pending"] } }` |
| `$nin` | Value is not in array | `{ status: { $nin: ["archived", "deleted"] } }` |

```typescript
{
  resource: "users",
  version: 1,
  filters: {
    role: { $in: ["admin", "moderator"] },
  },
}
```

## String Operators

| Operator | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `$contains` | String contains substring | `{ title: { $contains: "urgent" } }` |
| `$startsWith` | String starts with prefix | `{ email: { $startsWith: "admin" } }` |
| `$endsWith` | String ends with suffix | `{ email: { $endsWith: ".com" } }` |
| `$like` | SQL LIKE pattern (case-sensitive) | `{ title: { $like: "%shop%" } }` |
| `$ilike` | SQL LIKE pattern (case-insensitive) | `{ title: { $ilike: "%SHOP%" } }` |
| `$not_like` | Negated LIKE (case-sensitive) | `{ title: { $not_like: "%draft%" } }` |
| `$not_ilike` | Negated LIKE (case-insensitive) | `{ title: { $not_ilike: "%DRAFT%" } }` |

The `$like` and `$ilike` operators use SQL LIKE syntax: `%` matches any sequence of characters, `_` matches a single character. In the client-side evaluator, these patterns are converted to regular expressions via `likeToRegExp()`.

```typescript
{
  resource: "articles",
  version: 1,
  filters: {
    title: { $ilike: "%typescript%" },
    slug: { $startsWith: "2024-" },
  },
}
```

The `$contains` operator also works on array fields, checking whether the array includes the specified value:

```typescript
// Match records where the tags array contains "important"
{ tags: { $contains: "important" } }
```

## Null and Empty Operators

| Operator | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `$is_null` | Value is null or undefined | `{ deletedAt: { $is_null: true } }` |
| `$is_not_null` | Value is not null/undefined | `{ assignedTo: { $is_not_null: true } }` |
| `$is_empty` | Value is null, undefined, empty string, or empty array | `{ description: { $is_empty: true } }` |
| `$is_not_empty` | Opposite of $is_empty | `{ description: { $is_not_empty: true } }` |

These operators accept a boolean value. Pass `true` to assert the condition, `false` to negate it:

```typescript
// Records where deletedAt IS null
{ deletedAt: { $is_null: true } }

// Records where deletedAt IS NOT null (equivalent)
{ deletedAt: { $is_null: false } }
```

## Range Operators

| Operator | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `$between` | Value is within [low, high] (inclusive) | `{ age: { $between: [18, 65] } }` |
| `$not_between` | Value is outside [low, high] | `{ age: { $not_between: [18, 65] } }` |
| `$before` | Value is strictly less than (alias for date/time semantics) | `{ createdAt: { $before: 1700000000000 } }` |
| `$after` | Value is strictly greater than | `{ createdAt: { $after: 1700000000000 } }` |

```typescript
{
  resource: "orders",
  version: 1,
  filters: {
    total: { $between: [100, 500] },
    createdAt: { $after: 1700000000000 },
  },
}
```

`$between` and `$not_between` require a two-element array `[low, high]`. The check is inclusive on both ends.

## Logical Operators

Combine multiple filter conditions using `$and` and `$or`:

```typescript
// $and: all conditions must match (this is the default for top-level keys)
{
  filters: {
    $and: [
      { status: "active" },
      { priority: { $gte: 3 } },
    ],
  },
}

// $or: at least one condition must match
{
  filters: {
    $or: [
      { completed: true },
      { priority: { $gte: 5 } },
    ],
  },
}
```

Logical operators can be nested:

```typescript
{
  filters: {
    $or: [
      {
        $and: [
          { status: "active" },
          { priority: { $gte: 5 } },
        ],
      },
      { assignedTo: { $is_null: true } },
    ],
  },
}
```

Filter nesting depth is capped at 10 levels to prevent abuse.

## Relation Quantifier Filters (Server-Side)

On the server, filters can target related records using quantifier operators. These are evaluated against the related records resolved through schema-defined relations.

| Operator | Description |
|---|---|
| `$any` | At least one related record matches the sub-filter |
| `$all` | All related records match the sub-filter (false if no related records exist) |
| `$none` | No related records match the sub-filter (true if no related records exist) |

```typescript
// Find users who have at least one completed todo
{
  resource: "users",
  version: 1,
  filters: {
    todos: {
      $any: { completed: true },
    },
  },
}

// Find categories where ALL items are in stock
{
  resource: "categories",
  version: 1,
  filters: {
    items: {
      $all: { inStock: true },
    },
  },
}

// Find users with no overdue tasks
{
  resource: "users",
  version: 1,
  filters: {
    tasks: {
      $none: { overdue: true },
    },
  },
}
```

## Dot-Path Filters

Filters can traverse nested object fields using dot notation:

```typescript
// Filter on a nested object field
{ "address.city": "London" }

// Filter on a relation field (requires resolveRelation)
{ "author.name": "Alice" }
```

When the first segment of a dot-path does not resolve to a field on the record, the evaluator attempts to resolve it as a relation (if a relation resolver is provided).

## Programmatic Filter Evaluation

The `evaluateFilter` function evaluates a filter against a single record in memory. This is used by the client's offline query engine and the server's in-memory execution path.

```typescript
import { evaluateFilter } from "@datafn/core";

const record = { id: "1", title: "Test", priority: 3, completed: false };

evaluateFilter(record, { priority: { $gte: 2 }, completed: false });
// true

evaluateFilter(record, { priority: { $gt: 5 } });
// false
```

For server-side evaluation with relation support, pass a `FilterEvalOptions` object:

```typescript
evaluateFilter(record, filters, {
  resource: "todos",
  resolveRelation: (resource, recordId, relationName) => {
    // Return array of related records
    return relatedRecords;
  },
});
```



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Mutations

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/mutations
Description: DFQL write operations, including capability-aware lifecycle and sharing mutations.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A DFQL mutation is a write operation against a resource.

## Mutation Shape

```typescript
type DfqlMutation = {
  resource: string;
  version: number;
  operation: string;
  id?: string | string[];
  record?: Record<string, unknown>;
  records?: Array<Record<string, unknown>>;
  clientId?: string;
  mutationId?: string;
  context?: unknown;
  relations?: Record<string, unknown>;
  if?: Record<string, unknown>;
  cascade?: unknown;
  silent?: boolean;
  system?: boolean;
  debounceKey?: string;
  debounceMs?: number;
  scope?: "record" | "resource";
  shareWith?: { principalId: string; level?: string };
};
```

In direct server requests, `id` is expected for mutation operations. When using table handles, IDs for `insert` can be auto-generated client-side.

## Supported Operations

### Core operations

| Operation | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `insert` | Create a new record |
| `merge` | Partial update (upsert semantics) |
| `replace` | Replace full record contents |
| `delete` | Hard-delete record |

### Capability operations

These are valid only when the target resource enables the required capability.

| Operation | Requires capability | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `trash` | `trash` | Mark record as trashed (`trashedAt`, `trashedBy`) |
| `restore` | `trash` | Clear trash markers |
| `archive` | `archivable` | Set `isArchived: true` |
| `unarchive` | `archivable` | Set `isArchived: false` |
| `share` | `shareable` | Grant user access level on a record |
| `unshare` | `shareable` | Remove user access |

### Relation operations

| Operation | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `relate` | Create/update relation edges |
| `modifyRelation` | Update relation metadata on existing edge |
| `unrelate` | Remove relation edges |

## Core Examples

### Insert

```typescript
{
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  operation: "insert",
  id: "td:1",
  record: {
    title: "Buy groceries",
    completed: false,
  },
}
```

### Merge

```typescript
{
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  operation: "merge",
  id: "td:1",
  record: {
    completed: true,
  },
}
```

### Replace

```typescript
{
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  operation: "replace",
  id: "td:1",
  record: {
    title: "Updated task",
    completed: false,
    priority: 1,
  },
}
```

Fields omitted from a `replace` record are reset: a field with a `default`
gets that value, and every other field is cleared. Cleared fields are
persisted as `null` — the only clear representation every supported storage
adapter applies and that survives JSON change tracking — and are exposed as
`undefined` in query results unless the field is `nullable`.

### Delete

```typescript
{
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  operation: "delete",
  id: "td:1",
}
```

When the deleted record is referenced by relations that declare an [`onDelete` policy](/docs/dfql/schema/relations#delete-policies), the server enforces that policy as part of the delete:

- `restrict` — the delete fails with `RELATION_RESTRICTED` if referencing rows exist.
- `cascade` — referencing records are deleted recursively.
- `setNull` / `detach` — referencing foreign keys are cleared (and many-many join rows removed).

## Capability Examples

### Trash / Restore

```typescript
{ resource: "todos", version: 1, operation: "trash", id: "td:1" }
{ resource: "todos", version: 1, operation: "restore", id: "td:1" }
```

### Archive / Unarchive

```typescript
{ resource: "todos", version: 1, operation: "archive", id: "td:1" }
{ resource: "todos", version: 1, operation: "unarchive", id: "td:1" }
```

### Share / Unshare

#### Record-level share (default)

```typescript
{
  resource: "documents",
  version: 1,
  operation: "share",
  id: "doc:1",
  shareWith: { principalId: "user:alice", level: "editor" },
}

{
  resource: "documents",
  version: 1,
  operation: "unshare",
  id: "doc:1",
  shareWith: { principalId: "user:alice" },
}
```

#### Resource-level scope grant

When `supportsScopeGrants` is enabled on the shareable capability, you can grant access to all records in a resource:

```typescript
{
  resource: "documents",
  version: 1,
  operation: "share",
  scope: "resource",
  shareWith: { principalId: "team:engineering", level: "viewer" },
}
```

The `scope` field accepts `"record"` (default) or `"resource"`. When `scope` is `"resource"`, omit `id` — the grant applies to all records in the resource namespace.

#### `shareWith` fields

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `principalId` | `string` | **(recommended)** Target principal in `type:id` format (e.g. `"user:alice"`, `"team:ops"`). |
| `userId` | `string` | **(deprecated)** Legacy field. Canonicalized to `principalId` at runtime (`"alice"` becomes `"user:alice"`). Emits a deprecation warning. |
| `level` | `string` | Access level from the capability's `levels` array. Defaults to `"viewer"` if omitted on `share`. |

> **Migration note:** `shareWith.userId` is accepted for backward compatibility but triggers a deprecation warning. Update all call sites to use `shareWith.principalId`.

## Readonly Capability Fields

When `timestamps`, `audit`, or `trash` are enabled, the server strips client-provided values for readonly capability fields from `record`.

Examples of stripped fields:

- `createdAt`, `updatedAt`
- `createdBy`, `updatedBy`
- `trashedAt`, `trashedBy`

Server-generated values are authoritative.

## Foreign Key Normalization

When a record is written (`insert`, `merge`, `replace`, or via sync push), DataFn normalizes **optional** relation foreign-key fields: an empty string `""` is stored as `null`. This applies to the FK field and its paired polymorphic `*Resource` discriminator field. Required FK fields are left unchanged.

This keeps "unset" foreign keys consistent so relation queries and [delete policies](/docs/dfql/schema/relations#delete-policies) treat them as absent.

## Batch Mutations

You can send arrays of mutations.

```typescript
[
  { resource: "todos", version: 1, operation: "insert", id: "td:1", record: { title: "First" } },
  { resource: "todos", version: 1, operation: "insert", id: "td:2", record: { title: "Second" } },
]
```

## Guard Clause (`if`)

`if` enables conditional writes. The mutation executes only if the guard matches current row state.

```typescript
{
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  operation: "merge",
  id: "td:1",
  record: { status: "completed" },
  if: { status: "in_progress" },
}
```

## Silent, System, Context, Debounce

```typescript
{
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  operation: "merge",
  id: "td:1",
  record: { title: "Typing..." },
  context: { source: "editor" },
  silent: false,
  system: false,
  debounceKey: "td:1:title",
  debounceMs: 1500,
}
```

## Related Docs

- [Capabilities](/docs/documentation/capabilities)
- [System Fields](/docs/dfql/schema/system-fields)
- [Relations](/docs/dfql/schema/relations)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Pagination

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/pagination
Description: Paginate query results with limit/offset or cursors.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DFQL supports two pagination modes: limit/offset and cursor-based. Both can be combined with sorting and filtering.

## Limit/Offset Pagination

The simplest pagination mode. Set `limit` to cap the number of returned records and `offset` to skip records.

```typescript
// First page
const page1: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  sort: ["createdAt:desc"],
  limit: 20,
  offset: 0,
};

// Second page
const page2: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  sort: ["createdAt:desc"],
  limit: 20,
  offset: 20,
};
```

Limit/offset is straightforward but has a known limitation: for large offsets, the database must scan and discard all preceding rows, which degrades performance. For large datasets, prefer cursor-based pagination.

## Cursor-Based Pagination

Cursor pagination uses sort-field values from a boundary record to efficiently seek to the next page. It avoids the performance cliff of large offsets.

### Cursor Structure

```typescript
type DfqlCursor = {
  after?: Record<string, unknown>;  // Fetch records after this position
  before?: Record<string, unknown>; // Fetch records before this position
};
```

The cursor object contains the sort-field values of the boundary record. For example, if sorting by `["createdAt:desc", "id:asc"]`, the cursor contains `{ createdAt: ..., id: ... }`.

### Forward Pagination

```typescript
// First page
const page1: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  sort: ["createdAt:desc", "id:asc"],
  limit: 20,
};
// Response: { data: [...], nextCursor: { createdAt: 1700000000, id: "todo_42" } }

// Next page: use nextCursor as cursor.after
const page2: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  sort: ["createdAt:desc", "id:asc"],
  limit: 20,
  cursor: {
    after: { createdAt: 1700000000, id: "todo_42" },
  },
};
```

### Backward Pagination

Use `cursor.before` to paginate backward:

```typescript
const prevPage: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  sort: ["createdAt:desc", "id:asc"],
  limit: 20,
  cursor: {
    before: { createdAt: 1700050000, id: "todo_10" },
  },
};
```

### How nextCursor is Computed

The server internally fetches `limit + 1` records. If more than `limit` records are returned, a next page exists and `nextCursor` is computed from the sort-field values of the last record on the current page. If exactly `limit` or fewer records are returned, `nextCursor` is `null`.

### Performance

The cursor implementation uses binary search to find the first record after the cursor position in already-sorted result sets. This gives `O(log n)` seek time compared to `O(n)` for a linear scan.

## Count Queries

Set `count: true` to include a total count of matching records (before pagination) in the response:

```typescript
const query: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  filters: { completed: false },
  count: true,
  limit: 10,
};
// Response: { data: [...], count: 42, nextCursor: ... }
```

On the server with push-down queries, count is executed via a separate `db.count()` call with the same filter conditions. For in-memory queries, count is derived from the filtered record set before pagination is applied.

## Combining Pagination Modes

Limit/offset and cursor pagination are best treated as separate modes. If both `offset` and `cursor` are provided, the cursor window is applied first and any `offset` is still applied afterward, which can skip additional items unexpectedly.

## Sort Requirement for Cursors

Cursor pagination requires a sort order that includes `id` as a tiebreaker to ensure deterministic positioning. If the sort does not include an `id` field, the server returns a validation error.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Queries

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/queries
Description: Retrieve data with DFQL queries.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A DFQL query is a JSON object that describes what data to retrieve from a resource. Queries support filtering, sorting, pagination, field selection, aggregation, search, and cancellation.

## Query Structure

```typescript
type DfqlQuery = {
  resource: string;         // Target resource name
  version: number;          // Schema version
  select?: string[];        // Fields and relations to include
  omit?: string[];          // Fields to exclude
  filters?: Record<string, unknown>;  // Filter conditions
  search?: Record<string, unknown>;   // Full-text search block
  sort?: string[];          // Sort terms
  limit?: number;           // Maximum records to return
  offset?: number;          // Skip N records (limit/offset pagination)
  cursor?: DfqlCursor;      // Cursor pagination
  count?: boolean;          // Include total count in response
  groupBy?: string[];       // Group results by fields
  aggregations?: Record<string, unknown>; // Aggregate functions
  having?: Record<string, unknown>;       // Filter on aggregated groups
  signal?: AbortSignal;     // Cancel the query
};
```

## Basic Queries

Retrieve all records from a resource:

```typescript
const query: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
};
```

Add filters, sorting, and pagination:

```typescript
const query: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  filters: { completed: false },
  sort: ["priority:desc", "createdAt:asc"],
  limit: 20,
  offset: 0,
};
```

## Count Queries

Request a total count alongside results by setting `count: true`:

```typescript
const query: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  filters: { completed: false },
  count: true,
  limit: 10,
};
// Response includes: { data: [...], count: 42, nextCursor: ... }
```

## Batch Queries

Pass an array of queries to execute multiple queries in a single request:

```typescript
const queries: DfqlQuery[] = [
  { resource: "todos", version: 1, filters: { completed: false } },
  { resource: "users", version: 1, limit: 10 },
];
```

## Cancellation

Pass an `AbortSignal` to cancel a query in progress:

```typescript
const controller = new AbortController();

const query: DfqlQuery = {
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  signal: controller.signal,
};

// Cancel the query
controller.abort();
```

## Query Normalization

DFQL queries can be normalized to a canonical form for caching and comparison. This is useful when the same logical query is constructed from different code paths that may produce different key orderings.

```typescript
import { normalizeDfql, dfqlKey } from "@datafn/core";

const key = dfqlKey({
  resource: "todos",
  version: 1,
  filters: { completed: false },
});
// Produces a deterministic string: sorted keys, undefined stripped
```

`normalizeDfql` sorts object keys alphabetically and removes `undefined` values. `dfqlKey` wraps this in `JSON.stringify` to produce a stable cache key.

## Server-Side Query Classification

On the server, queries are classified into one of three execution strategies:

| Strategy | Description |
|---|---|
| **Full pushdown** | The adapter handles the primary-resource query path directly. This is used only for query shapes that stay within adapter-supported filters, sorting, and pagination. |
| **Partial pushdown** | The primary resource can be fetched efficiently, but relation expansion or projection work still happens in memory after the adapter returns rows. |
| **In-memory** | DataFn loads candidate rows and completes filtering, sorting, pagination, grouping, or projection in memory. This is required for aggregation, `groupBy`, server-side search, and query shapes the adapter cannot safely push down. |

The classification is automatic and transparent. The server always selects the most efficient strategy for a given query shape.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Fields

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/schema/fields
Description: Configure field types, validation constraints, and behavior.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## DatafnFieldSchema

Each field in a resource defines its name, type, and field metadata. Core
mutation validation enforces field types and nullability on the server.

```typescript
type DatafnFieldSchema = {
  name: string;
  type:
    | "string"
    | "number"
    | "boolean"
    | "date"
    | "object"
    | "array"
    | "file"
    | "json";
  required: boolean;
  nullable?: boolean;
  readonly?: boolean;
  default?: unknown;
  enum?: unknown[];
  min?: number;
  max?: number;
  minLength?: number;
  maxLength?: number;
  pattern?: string;
  unique?: boolean | string;
  encrypt?: boolean;
  volatile?: boolean;
};
```

## Field Types

| Type      | TypeScript                | Storage  | Notes                                                                          |
| --------- | ------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `string`  | `string`                  | Text     | General-purpose text values.                                                   |
| `number`  | `number`                  | Numeric  | NaN is rejected during validation.                                             |
| `boolean` | `boolean`                 | Boolean  | Strict `true`/`false` only.                                                    |
| `date`    | `string \| number`        | Epoch ms | Accepts ISO 8601 strings or epoch milliseconds. Stored as epoch ms internally. ISO datetimes without a timezone designator are interpreted as UTC, so validation and storage resolve the same instant in any server timezone. |
| `object`  | `Record<string, unknown>` | JSON     | Plain objects only. Arrays are rejected; `null` requires `nullable: true`.     |
| `array`   | `unknown[]`               | JSON     | Array values only.                                                             |
| `file`    | `string`                  | Text     | File reference (URL or path). Validated as a string.                           |
| `json`    | `unknown`                 | JSON     | Any JSON value; `null` requires `nullable: true`.                              |

## Const-safe field builders

Use `field` for reusable fields and `defineSchema` for the complete schema.
Builders return plain `DatafnFieldSchema` objects, preserve literal names and
enum members, and emit explicit `required: false` and `nullable: false`
defaults.

```typescript
import { defineSchema, field } from "@datafn/core";

const id = field.string("id", { required: true, unique: true });
const sharedFields = [
  field.boolean("isStarred", { default: false }),
  field.file("attachment"),
];

export const schema = defineSchema({
  resources: [
    {
      name: "tasks",
      version: 1,
      fields: [
        id,
        field.string("status", {
          required: true,
          enum: ["NOT_STARTED", "IN_PROGRESS", "COMPLETED"],
        }),
        ...sharedFields,
      ],
      indices: { base: ["id", "status", "isStarred"] },
    },
  ],
});
```

Requiredness controls whether the record property is present. Nullability
independently controls whether its value includes `null`. Inline object
literals passed directly to `defineSchema` preserve the same inference.
Explicitly annotating a schema as `DatafnSchema` or a reusable array as
`DatafnFieldSchema[]` widens literal information; use `satisfies` for an
assignability check without widening, or use field builders.

Builder options are specific to each field kind. Incompatible defaults, enum
values, bounds, and misspelled options fail type checking. `name` and `type`
are owned by the selected builder and cannot be overridden.

## Constraints

Constraint metadata is preserved for adapters and generated schemas. Core
mutation validation enforces `min`/`max` bounds for `date` fields (compared
as epoch milliseconds) but does not currently enforce every other
constraint, including enum membership, number bounds, and patterns. Check
the selected storage adapter before relying on those constraints at runtime.

### required

When `true`, the field must be present and non-undefined in insert mutations. Fields with a `default` value satisfy the required check automatically.

```typescript
{ name: "title", type: "string", required: true }
```

### nullable

When `true`, the field accepts `null` as a valid value. By default, `null` is rejected for all types.

```typescript
{ name: "deletedAt", type: "date", required: false, nullable: true }
```

### readonly

When `true`, the field can be set on insert but cannot be modified by subsequent update or merge mutations.

```typescript
{ name: "createdBy", type: "string", required: true, readonly: true }
```

### default

A default value applied when the field is omitted from an insert mutation.

```typescript
{ name: "status", type: "string", required: true, default: "draft" }
{ name: "viewCount", type: "number", required: true, default: 0 }
```

### enum

Restricts the field to a fixed set of allowed values.

```typescript
{ name: "priority", type: "string", required: true, enum: ["low", "medium", "high", "critical"] }
```

### min / max

Numeric range constraints. Apply to `number` and `date` fields.

```typescript
{ name: "score", type: "number", required: true, min: 0, max: 100 }
```

### minLength / maxLength

String length constraints. Apply to `string` fields.

```typescript
{ name: "username", type: "string", required: true, minLength: 3, maxLength: 64 }
```

### pattern

A regular expression pattern the string value must match.

```typescript
{ name: "slug", type: "string", required: true, pattern: "^[a-z0-9-]+$" }
```

### unique

When `true`, enforces a unique constraint on the field across all records in the resource. When set to a string, it defines a named uniqueness group -- fields sharing the same group name form a composite unique constraint.

```typescript
// Simple unique constraint
{ name: "email", type: "string", required: true, unique: true }

// Composite unique constraint -- (orgId, slug) must be unique together
{ name: "orgId", type: "string", required: true, unique: "org_slug" }
{ name: "slug", type: "string", required: true, unique: "org_slug" }
```

### encrypt

When `true`, the field value is encrypted at rest. Useful for sensitive data like tokens or personal information.

```typescript
{ name: "apiKey", type: "string", required: true, encrypt: true }
```

### volatile

When `true`, the field is excluded from sync operations. Volatile fields exist only in the local client store and are not pushed to the server.

```typescript
{ name: "localDraft", type: "string", required: false, volatile: true }
```

## Complete Example

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

const schema = defineSchema({
  resources: [
    {
      name: "users",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "usr",
      fields: [
        {
          name: "email",
          type: "string",
          required: true,
          unique: true,
          maxLength: 255,
        },
        {
          name: "displayName",
          type: "string",
          required: true,
          minLength: 1,
          maxLength: 100,
        },
        {
          name: "role",
          type: "string",
          required: true,
          enum: ["admin", "editor", "viewer"],
          default: "viewer",
        },
        {
          name: "bio",
          type: "string",
          required: false,
          maxLength: 2000,
          nullable: true,
        },
        {
          name: "loginCount",
          type: "number",
          required: true,
          default: 0,
          min: 0,
        },
        {
          name: "emailVerified",
          type: "boolean",
          required: true,
          default: false,
        },
        { name: "lastLoginAt", type: "date", required: false, nullable: true },
        { name: "avatar", type: "file", required: false },
        { name: "preferences", type: "json", required: false },
        { name: "settings", type: "object", required: false },
        { name: "favoriteTopics", type: "array", required: false },
        {
          name: "encryptedToken",
          type: "string",
          required: false,
          encrypt: true,
        },
        { name: "localNotes", type: "string", required: false, volatile: true },
      ],
      indices: {
        base: ["email", "role"],
        search: ["displayName", "bio"],
      },
    },
  ],
});
```



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Schema Definition

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/schema
Description: Define and validate your DataFn schema, including capability-driven behavior.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## DatafnSchema

A DataFn schema defines resources, relations, and optional global capabilities.

```typescript
type DatafnSchema = {
  capabilities?: SchemaCapabilities;
  resources: DatafnResourceSchema[];
  relations?: DatafnRelationSchema[];
  relationIntegrity?: "application" | "database";
  namespaced?: boolean; // defaults to true
};
```

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `capabilities` | `SchemaCapabilities` | Optional global capability entries applied to resources by default. |
| `resources` | `DatafnResourceSchema[]` | Resource definitions (required, max 100). |
| `relations` | `DatafnRelationSchema[]` | Optional relation definitions (`[]` when omitted). |
| `relationIntegrity` | `"application" \| "database"` | Default [relation integrity](/docs/dfql/schema/relations#relation-integrity) mode for all relations. Defaults to `"application"`. The removed `"hybrid"` mode is rejected. |
| `namespaced` | `boolean` | Namespace isolation flag (defaults to `true`). |

See [Capabilities](/docs/documentation/capabilities) for the behavior model.

## defineSchema

`defineSchema` gives compile-time safety for field names, index fields, and capability declarations.

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

const schema = defineSchema({
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit"],
  resources: [
    {
      name: "projects",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "prj",
      capabilities: ["archivable"],
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true, maxLength: 200 },
        { name: "status", type: "string", required: true, enum: ["active", "done"] },
      ],
      indices: { base: ["title", "status"] },
    },
    {
      name: "auditLogs",
      version: 1,
      capabilities: { exclude: ["audit"] },
      fields: [{ name: "message", type: "string", required: true }],
    },
  ],
});
```

## validateSchema

`validateSchema(schema)` performs runtime validation and normalization and returns `DatafnEnvelope<DatafnSchema>`.

```typescript
import { validateSchema } from "@datafn/core";

const result = validateSchema(schema);
if (!result.ok) {
  console.error(result.error.code, result.error.message);
}
```

### Normalization

On success, DataFn normalizes:

- capability arrays (deduped and canonicalized),
- `indices: string[]` to `{ base, search, vector }`,
- omitted `relations` to `[]`,
- omitted `namespaced` to `true`.

### Validation checks

`validateSchema` enforces:

- resource structure and limits (max 100 resources, max 200 fields/resource),
- unique resource names and field names,
- index fields must exist,
- relation references must point to declared resources,
- capability declarations and capability config validity,
- capability field collisions (`CAPABILITY_FIELD_COLLISION`),
- capability dependencies (for example `shareable` requires `audit`),
- relation capability constraints (`many-many` only, `timestamps|audit` only),
- relation integrity mode (`"application"` or `"database"`; the legacy `"hybrid"` mode is rejected),
- relation delete policies (`onDelete` must be a valid policy or `{ from?, to? }` object).

## Namespace default

`namespaced` defaults to `true`. Only explicit `namespaced: false` disables row-level namespace isolation.

```typescript
import { isNamespaced } from "@datafn/core";

isNamespaced(schema); // true by default
```



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Relations

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/dfql/schema/relations
Description: Define, query, and mutate relationships between resources.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Defining Relations

Relations define how resources are connected. DataFn supports four relation types: `one-many`, `many-one`, `many-many`, and `htree` (hierarchical tree).

```typescript
type DatafnRelationSchema = {
  from: string | string[];
  to: string | string[];
  type: "one-many" | "many-one" | "many-many" | "htree";
  relation?: string;
  inverse?: string;
  cache?: boolean;
  capabilities?: Array<"timestamps" | "audit">;
  metadata?: Array<{
    name: string;
    type: "string" | "number" | "boolean" | "date" | "object" | "json";
  }>;
  fkField?: string;
  fkResourceField?: string;
  pathField?: string;
  joinTable?: string;
  joinColumns?: { from: string; to: string };
  integrity?: "application" | "database";
  onDelete?: DatafnRelationDeletePolicies;
};

type DatafnRelationDeletePolicy = "restrict" | "cascade" | "setNull" | "detach";
type DatafnRelationDeletePolicies =
  | DatafnRelationDeletePolicy
  | { from?: DatafnRelationDeletePolicy; to?: DatafnRelationDeletePolicy };
```

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `from` | `string \| string[]` | Source resource name(s). An array declares a [polymorphic](#polymorphic-relations) endpoint. |
| `to` | `string \| string[]` | Target resource name(s). An array declares a [polymorphic](#polymorphic-relations) endpoint. |
| `type` | `string` | Relation cardinality. |
| `relation` | `string` | Optional name for the forward relation. |
| `inverse` | `string` | Optional name for the inverse relation. |
| `cache` | `boolean` | When `true`, enables relation caching for performance. |
| `capabilities` | `Array<"timestamps" \| "audit">` | Server-managed capability fields on the join row (many-many only, explicit opt-in). |
| `metadata` | `Array` | Extra fields stored on the join record (many-many only). |
| `fkField` | `string` | Foreign key field name override for one-many / many-one / htree. |
| `fkResourceField` | `string` | Discriminator field that stores the target resource name for a [polymorphic](#polymorphic-relations) FK side. |
| `pathField` | `string` | Materialized path field for htree relations (default `parentPath`). |
| `joinTable` | `string` | Explicit join table name for many-many relations. |
| `joinColumns` | `{ from, to }` | Column name overrides for the join table. |
| `integrity` | `"application" \| "database"` | Per-relation override of [relation integrity](#relation-integrity). |
| `onDelete` | `DatafnRelationDeletePolicies` | [Delete policy](#delete-policies) applied when a referenced record is deleted. |

### One-to-Many

A single record in the `from` resource relates to multiple records in the `to` resource. The foreign key is stored on the `to` side.

```typescript
const schema = defineSchema({
  resources: [
    {
      name: "authors",
      version: 1,
      fields: [
        { name: "name", type: "string", required: true },
      ],
    },
    {
      name: "books",
      version: 1,
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "authorId", type: "string", required: true },
      ],
      indices: { base: ["authorId"] },
    },
  ],
  relations: [
    {
      from: "authors",
      to: "books",
      type: "one-many",
      relation: "authorBooks",
      fkField: "authorId",
    },
  ],
});
```

### Many-to-One

The inverse of one-to-many. Multiple records in the `from` resource point to a single record in the `to` resource.

```typescript
relations: [
  {
    from: "books",
    to: "authors",
    type: "many-one",
    relation: "bookAuthor",
    fkField: "authorId",
  },
]
```

### Many-to-Many

Both sides can have multiple related records. DataFn uses a join table to store the associations. You can add `metadata` fields to the join record.

```typescript
const schema = defineSchema({
  resources: [
    {
      name: "students",
      version: 1,
      fields: [
        { name: "name", type: "string", required: true },
      ],
    },
    {
      name: "courses",
      version: 1,
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
      ],
    },
  ],
  relations: [
    {
      from: "students",
      to: "courses",
      type: "many-many",
      relation: "enrollments",
      joinTable: "student_courses",
      joinColumns: { from: "student_id", to: "course_id" },
      metadata: [
        { name: "enrolledAt", type: "date" },
        { name: "grade", type: "string" },
      ],
    },
  ],
});
```

The `metadata` array defines additional columns on the join table. These fields are stored alongside the association and can be read when querying the relation.

### Relation Capabilities
