## Recipes
================================================================================


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Audit Logging

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/audit-logging
Description: Capability-driven audit fields plus outbound logging to your audit pipeline.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DataFn ships two complementary audit primitives:

1. The **`audit` capability** that injects `createdBy` and `updatedBy` on every resource.
2. The **plugin hook system** that runs after every mutation, perfect for pushing audit events to your logging pipeline.

For compliance use cases (SOC 2, HIPAA, ISO 27001) you want both. The capability gives you a quick "who changed this row" answer in the database; the outbound stream gives you an immutable append-only log that survives database tampering.

## Step 1: Enable the audit capability

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export const schema = defineSchema({
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit"],
  resources: [
    { name: "documents", version: 1, idPrefix: "doc", fields: [/* ... */] },
  ],
});
```

This injects `createdBy` and `updatedBy` (managed system fields). To populate them, supply a `namespaceProvider` with `getActorId`:

```typescript
namespaceProvider: {
  getNamespace: (ctx) => ns(ctx.session.orgId),
  getActorId:  (ctx) => ctx.session.userId,
},
```

Now every row carries the user id of the last writer. Reading is free:

```typescript
const docs = await client.table("documents").query({
  filters: { id: { $eq: docId } },
  select: ["id", "title", "createdBy", "updatedBy", "updatedAt"],
});
```

## Step 2: Push to an outbound log

Audit-grade systems want an **append-only** log that's hard to tamper with. Use a `afterMutation` hook:

```typescript
import type { DatafnPlugin } from "@datafn/core";
import { logToSiem } from "./siem"; // your audit pipeline

export const auditPlugin: DatafnPlugin = {
  name: "audit-log",
  hooks: [
    {
      event: "afterMutation",
      handler: async (ctx) => {
        const mut = ctx.payload as DfqlMutation;
        await logToSiem({
          ts: Date.now(),
          actor: ctx.ctx?.session?.userId,
          namespace: ctx.ctx?.session?.orgId,
          resource: ctx.resource,
          operation: mut.operation,
          recordId: mut.id ?? mut.record?.id,
          before: ctx.meta?.before,    // if your hook captured it
          after: mut.record,
        });
      },
    },
    {
      event: "beforeMutation",
      handler: async (ctx) => {
        const mut = ctx.payload as DfqlMutation;
        if (mut.id) {
          const before = await server.db.findOne(ctx.resource, mut.id);
          ctx.meta = { ...ctx.meta, before };
        }
      },
    },
  ],
};
```

Drop into the server config:

```typescript
const datafn = await createDatafnServer({
  schema,
  db,
  plugins: [auditPlugin],
  namespaceProvider,
});
```

## Step 3: Choose a sink

| Sink | When |
| --- | --- |
| Cloud-native (CloudWatch, GCP Audit Logs, Azure Monitor) | You're already in that cloud; want minimal infra. |
| SIEM (Splunk, Datadog Cloud SIEM, Panther) | You have a security team; want correlation. |
| Append-only DB (DynamoDB with conditional writes, S3+Athena, BigQuery) | You need long retention and analytical queries. |
| Blockchain anchoring (rare; for highest tamper resistance) | Regulatory requirement. |

For most teams, a managed SIEM is the right call.

## Step 4: Read access logging

For some audits you need "who **read** this row" too. Add an `afterQuery` hook:

```typescript
{
  event: "afterQuery",
  filter: { resource: ["patients", "financials"] },
  handler: async (ctx) => {
    const result = ctx.payload as { data: any[] };
    if (!result.data.length) return;
    await logToSiem({
      ts: Date.now(),
      actor: ctx.ctx?.session?.userId,
      action: "read",
      resource: ctx.resource,
      ids: result.data.map((r) => r.id),
    });
  },
}
```

This pattern is heavy — every read produces a log entry. Use it only on truly sensitive resources, not as a general default.

## What not to do

- **Don't store audit logs in DataFn.** It's an OLTP sync layer, not a log store. Append-only writes at audit scale will balloon your changelog table.
- **Don't trust client-supplied actor ids.** Always derive `actor` from server-side context (`ctx.session.userId`).
- **Don't log sensitive payloads in plaintext.** Encrypt `before`/`after` if they include PII, or store only field-level diffs without values.

## See also

- [Capabilities](/docs/documentation/capabilities)
- [Custom Plugins](/docs/documentation/plugins/custom-plugins)
- [Encryption at rest](/docs/recipes/encryption-at-rest)
- [Security overview](/docs/documentation/security)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: AuthFn Integration

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/authfn-integration
Description: Wire AuthFn sessions into DataFn's authorize and namespaceProvider.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AuthFn is the auth layer in the Superfunctions stack. It handles sign-in, session management, organizations, and roles. DataFn doesn't ship its own auth — it asks two callbacks for the relevant facts:

- `authorize(ctx, action, payload)` → can this request happen?
- `namespaceProvider.getNamespace(ctx)` / `getActorId(ctx)` → who's the actor and which tenant?

This recipe shows the canonical wiring.

## 1. Middleware: populate ctx.session

The Hono pattern (other frameworks are analogous — see the [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart) per framework):

```typescript
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { authfnSession } from "@authfn/server";

const app = new Hono();

app.use("*", async (c, next) => {
  const session = await authfnSession(c.req.raw);
  c.set("session", session ?? undefined);
  await next();
});
```

The shape of `session` from AuthFn:

```typescript
type AuthfnSession = {
  userId: string;
  orgId?: string;
  email: string;
  roles: string[]; // e.g. ["owner", "billing-admin"]
  expiresAt: number;
};
```

## 2. authorize: gate per action

```typescript
import { createDatafnServer } from "@datafn/server";

const datafn = await createDatafnServer({
  schema,
  db,
  authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
    const session = ctx.get("session") as AuthfnSession | undefined;
    if (!session) return false;

    // Free actions: status, search
    if (action === "status" || action === "search") return true;

    // Write actions need at least one role
    if (["mutation", "transact", "push"].includes(action) && session.roles.length === 0) {
      return false;
    }

    // Resource-level rules
    if (payload?.resource === "billing" && !session.roles.includes("billing-admin")) {
      return false;
    }

    return true;
  },
  namespaceProvider: {
    getNamespace: (ctx) => {
      const session = ctx.get("session") as AuthfnSession | undefined;
      return session?.orgId ? `org:${session.orgId}` : `user:${session?.userId}`;
    },
    getActorId: (ctx) => (ctx.get("session") as AuthfnSession | undefined)?.userId,
  },
});

app.route("/", toHono(datafn.router));
```

## 3. Personal vs organization context

Most apps need both modes. A user has a personal workspace plus zero-or-more orgs they belong to. The `orgId` switch happens in your AuthFn middleware (typically driven by a header or subdomain). The DataFn namespace then follows automatically — no changes needed in DataFn config.

## 4. Sharing across orgs

By default `crossNsShareable` is `false`, so a user in org A can't share with a user in org B. When you want cross-org sharing (e.g. external reviewers):

```typescript
{
  name: "documents",
  capabilities: [
    {
      name: "shareable",
      config: { crossNsShareable: true, roles: ["viewer", "editor"] },
    },
  ],
},
```

Now `share` operations with a principal id from another namespace succeed. The shared user sees the document in their own namespace's view.

## 5. Field-level authz

Some fields shouldn't be readable by all members. Use a `permissions` policy on the resource:

```typescript
{
  name: "users",
  permissions: {
    read: {
      "*": (ctx) => true,                     // any field by default
      "email": (ctx) => {
        const session = ctx.get("session") as AuthfnSession;
        return session.roles.includes("owner");
      },
      "salary": (ctx, row) => {
        const session = ctx.get("session") as AuthfnSession;
        return session.userId === row.id || session.roles.includes("owner");
      },
    },
  },
},
```

DataFn applies `permissions.read` per row, per field. Forbidden fields are silently elided from the response (not 403'd) — this is correct for list views where partial data is acceptable.

## 6. Sign-out

AuthFn handles sign-out. On the DataFn side, you typically:

1. Stop the client (`client.stop()` or `client.close()`).
2. Clear the IndexedDB store (`indexedDB.deleteDatabase("my-app-db")`) if the user is on a shared device.
3. Recreate the client on next sign-in.

The DataFn client doesn't have a "sign-out" call; the unit of identity is the `clientId`, which you assign at construction. For per-user devices, regenerate it on sign-in.

## 7. Testing the integration

```typescript
import { authfnTesting } from "@authfn/server/testing";

const session = authfnTesting.makeSession({ userId: "u_test", orgId: "o_test", roles: ["owner"] });
const ctx = new Map([["session", session]]);

const env = await datafn.router.fetch(
  new Request("http://t/datafn/query", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "x-test-context": JSON.stringify({ session }) },
    body: JSON.stringify({ resource: "tasks", version: 1 }),
  }),
);
```

For a thicker integration test, use `authfnTesting.signIn(...)` to produce a real session token and exercise the middleware path.

## See also

- [AuthFn docs](https://authfn.21n.co/docs)
- [Namespaces](/docs/documentation/namespaces)
- [Authorization](/docs/documentation/server/authorization)
- [Multi-tenant SaaS](/docs/recipes/multi-tenant-saas)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Chat App

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/chat-app
Description: Append-only messages, cursor pagination, WebSocket live updates.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A chat app is almost a special-case kanban: append-only inserts, ordered reads, and live tail. The pattern that matters is **cursor pagination** so an active conversation doesn't page-shift under the user.

## Schema

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export const schema = defineSchema({
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit"],
  resources: [
    {
      name: "rooms",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "rm",
      capabilities: ["shareable"],
      fields: [
        { name: "name", type: "string", required: true },
      ],
    },
    {
      name: "messages",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "msg",
      fields: [
        { name: "roomId", type: "string", required: true, references: { resource: "rooms" } },
        { name: "body", type: "string", required: true, maxLength: 2000 },
      ],
      indices: { base: ["roomId", "createdAt"] },
    },
  ],
});
```

Rooms are `shareable` so we can invite participants without an extra membership table. Messages have no soft-delete by default — add `trash` if you want it.

## Posting a message

```typescript
async function send(roomId: string, body: string) {
  await client.table("messages").mutate({
    operation: "insert",
    record: { roomId, body },
  });
}
```

The `audit` capability fills in `createdBy` automatically (so you know who sent the message), and `timestamps` fills in `createdAt`.

## Loading the conversation

Use cursor pagination — never offset. Offset shifts under inserts; cursor doesn't.

```typescript
const initial = await client.table("messages").query({
  filters: { roomId: { $eq: roomId } },
  sort: ["createdAt:desc", "id:desc"],
  limit: 30,
});

async function loadOlder(cursor: string) {
  return client.table("messages").query({
    filters: { roomId: { $eq: roomId } },
    sort: ["createdAt:desc", "id:desc"],
    limit: 30,
    cursor,
  });
}
```

In the UI, render `initial.data.reverse()` (newest at the bottom) and prepend `loadOlder` results to the top of the list.

## Live tail

```typescript
const tail = client.table("messages").signal({
  filters: { roomId: { $eq: roomId } },
  sort: ["createdAt:desc"],
  limit: 30,
});

tail.subscribe((value) => setMessages(value?.toReversed() ?? []));
```

The signal updates whenever a new message arrives — locally, from another tab, or from another participant via the WebSocket.

## Typing indicators

Typing indicators are ephemeral; don't persist them. Either:

1. **Use the WebSocket directly** — DataFn exposes the underlying WS for custom events. Send `{ type: "typing", roomId, userId }` and decay client-side after 5s.
2. **Use a tiny ephemeral resource** with a 60s TTL via a retention policy — heavier-weight but fits into the DFQL model.

For most apps, option 1 is correct. See [Presence and cursors](/docs/recipes/presence-cursors).

## Authorization

For room-level access control, use the `shareable` capability on `rooms`. Then in `messages`, defer to the parent room's visibility:

```typescript
authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
  if (payload?.resource === "messages") {
    const roomId =
      action === "query"
        ? payload.filters?.roomId?.$eq
        : payload.record?.roomId ?? payload.id;
    if (!roomId) return false;
    return userCanAccessRoom(ctx.user, roomId); // your function
  }
  return true;
};
```

The authorize callback can run DFQL itself to check the room's `shareable.principals`.

## Editing and deletion

Most chat apps support a 15-minute edit window. Use a server-side hook:

```typescript
plugins: [
  {
    name: "edit-window",
    hooks: [
      {
        event: "beforeMutation",
        filter: { resource: "messages", operation: ["merge", "replace", "delete"] },
        handler: async (ctx) => {
          const mut = ctx.payload as DfqlMutation;
          const original = await server.db.findOne("messages", mut.id);
          if (!original) return;
          if (Date.now() - original.createdAt > 15 * 60 * 1000) {
            return { abort: { code: "FORBIDDEN", message: "Edit window expired" } };
          }
        },
      },
    ],
  },
],
```

## See also

- [Sharing flows](/docs/recipes/sharing-flows)
- [WebSockets](/docs/documentation/server/websockets)
- [Pagination](/docs/dfql/pagination)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Document Collaboration

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/document-collab
Description: Per-document presence, conflict-free edits, and a roadmap to true CRDT collaboration.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DataFn is a sync engine, not a CRDT engine. For genuine concurrent text editing you want a CRDT library (Yjs, Automerge, Loro) layered on top — DataFn's job is to persist and broadcast the document state. This recipe shows the working pattern.

## Schema

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export const schema = defineSchema({
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit"],
  resources: [
    {
      name: "documents",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "doc",
      capabilities: ["shareable"],
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        // Snapshot: the latest serialized CRDT state, base64-encoded
        { name: "snapshot", type: "string", required: true },
        // Snapshot generation — monotonically increasing
        { name: "snapshotVersion", type: "number", required: true, default: 0 },
      ],
    },
    {
      name: "documentOps",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "op",
      fields: [
        { name: "documentId", type: "string", required: true, references: { resource: "documents" } },
        { name: "op", type: "string", required: true }, // base64-encoded CRDT update
      ],
      indices: { base: ["documentId", "createdAt"] },
    },
  ],
});
```

Two resources: `documents` for stable state and `documentOps` for the granular update log.

## The flow

1. Client loads `documents` row → restores Yjs/Automerge state from `snapshot`.
2. Client subscribes to `documentOps` filtered to this document.
3. As the user types, the CRDT emits binary updates; the client inserts each into `documentOps`.
4. Other clients receive the new ops via the WebSocket cursor → pull → signal.
5. Periodically (every 1k ops, or every 60s) one client wins a coordination dance and writes a fresh `snapshot` + truncates older ops.

## Loading a document

```typescript
import * as Y from "yjs";

async function openDocument(docId: string): Promise<Y.Doc> {
  const docs = await client.table("documents").query({
    filters: { id: { $eq: docId } },
  });
  const ydoc = new Y.Doc();
  if (docs.result.ok && docs.result.result.data[0]) {
    Y.applyUpdate(ydoc, base64Decode(docs.result.result.data[0].snapshot));
  }

  // Replay any ops written after the snapshot
  const ops = await client.table("documentOps").query({
    filters: {
      documentId: { $eq: docId },
      createdAt: { $gt: docs.result.result.data[0]?.updatedAt ?? 0 },
    },
    sort: ["createdAt:asc"],
  });

  for (const op of ops.result.result.data) {
    Y.applyUpdate(ydoc, base64Decode(op.op));
  }

  return ydoc;
}
```

## Writing edits

```typescript
ydoc.on("update", (update: Uint8Array) => {
  client.table("documentOps").mutate({
    operation: "insert",
    record: {
      documentId: docId,
      op: base64Encode(update),
    },
  });
});
```

Every Y.js update becomes one DataFn mutation. Mutations are batched by the sync engine, so high-frequency typing doesn't generate a flood of requests.

## Subscribing to remote ops

```typescript
const opSignal = client.table("documentOps").signal({
  filters: { documentId: { $eq: docId }, createdAt: { $gt: openedAt } },
  sort: ["createdAt:asc"],
});

opSignal.subscribe((ops) => {
  for (const op of ops ?? []) {
    if (op.createdBy === client.clientId) continue; // skip echoes
    Y.applyUpdate(ydoc, base64Decode(op.op));
  }
});
```

The `createdBy === clientId` skip is essential — without it you'll apply your own updates twice.

## Snapshotting

When `documentOps` grows past 1000 rows, snapshot:

```typescript
async function snapshot(docId: string, ydoc: Y.Doc) {
  const newSnapshot = base64Encode(Y.encodeStateAsUpdate(ydoc));
  await client.transact({
    steps: [
      {
        type: "mutation",
        mutation: {
          resource: "documents",
          version: 1,
          operation: "merge",
          id: docId,
          record: { snapshot: newSnapshot, snapshotVersion: nextVersion },
          if: { snapshotVersion: { $eq: currentVersion } },
        },
      },
    ],
  });
}
```

The `if` guard prevents two clients from racing to snapshot.

After the snapshot, older `documentOps` can be deleted by a server-side retention plugin — or left in place and queried only for the last snapshot's window.

## Presence

Cursor positions are ephemeral. Don't persist them — use the WebSocket directly. See [Presence and cursors](/docs/recipes/presence-cursors).

## Limitations

- DataFn doesn't yet have a binary field type, so CRDT state lives base64-encoded in a string field. Not the fastest. A binary type is on the roadmap.
- For very large documents, the snapshot field will exceed `limits.maxPayloadBytes`. Raise the limit or split the document.
- True multi-region presence under network partition is beyond DataFn's scope; pair with a presence server (PartyKit, Liveblocks).



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Encryption at Rest

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/encryption-at-rest
Description: Field-level encryption via plugins, with the server holding only ciphertext.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DataFn does not encrypt fields by default. The database handles disk-level encryption (Postgres encrypted volumes, SQLite encryption extensions), but values are stored plaintext in the row. For sensitive fields you can layer **field-level encryption** via a plugin, so the server never sees plaintext.

## When to use this

- **PII**: SSN, payment details, medical records.
- **End-to-end encryption** between users: only the recipients hold the key.
- **Defense-in-depth**: rate-limit blast radius if the database is exfiltrated.

When **not** to use this: if your server needs to filter or sort on the field. Encrypted fields are opaque — you can fetch them but you can't query them.

## Pattern: client-side WebCrypto

The simplest case is encrypting on the client before the mutation hits the wire.

```typescript
// shared/encryption.ts
const ALG = { name: "AES-GCM", length: 256 };

export async function encrypt(plaintext: string, key: CryptoKey): Promise<string> {
  const iv = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12));
  const enc = new TextEncoder().encode(plaintext);
  const ct = await crypto.subtle.encrypt({ name: "AES-GCM", iv }, key, enc);
  return btoa(JSON.stringify({ iv: Array.from(iv), ct: Array.from(new Uint8Array(ct)) }));
}

export async function decrypt(envelope: string, key: CryptoKey): Promise<string> {
  const { iv, ct } = JSON.parse(atob(envelope));
  const pt = await crypto.subtle.decrypt(
    { name: "AES-GCM", iv: new Uint8Array(iv) },
    key,
    new Uint8Array(ct).buffer,
  );
  return new TextDecoder().decode(pt);
}
```

Wire it as a client plugin:

```typescript
import type { DatafnPlugin } from "@datafn/core";

const encryptedFields = new Set(["ssn", "creditCard"]);

export function encryptionPlugin(key: CryptoKey): DatafnPlugin {
  return {
    name: "encryption-at-rest",
    hooks: [
      {
        event: "beforeMutation",
        handler: async (ctx) => {
          const mut = ctx.payload as DfqlMutation;
          if (!mut.record) return;
          const record = { ...mut.record };
          for (const field of Object.keys(record)) {
            if (encryptedFields.has(field) && typeof record[field] === "string") {
              record[field] = await encrypt(record[field] as string, key);
            }
          }
          return { ...mut, record };
        },
      },
      {
        event: "afterQuery",
        handler: async (ctx) => {
          const result = ctx.payload as { data: any[] };
          return {
            ...result,
            data: await Promise.all(
              result.data.map(async (row) => {
                const out = { ...row };
                for (const field of Object.keys(out)) {
                  if (encryptedFields.has(field) && typeof out[field] === "string") {
                    out[field] = await decrypt(out[field] as string, key);
                  }
                }
                return out;
              }),
            ),
          };
        },
      },
    ],
  };
}
```

Register on the client:

```typescript
const userKey = await deriveUserKey(); // your key management
const client = createDatafnClient({
  schema,
  clientId,
  storage,
  plugins: [encryptionPlugin(userKey)],
});
```

Now `ssn` and `creditCard` travel encrypted; the server stores opaque base64 blobs.

## Pattern: server-managed encryption

When the **server** is the trust boundary (PCI-style), keep the key in the server and decrypt only at egress. Mirror the same plugin on the server with a server-held key:

```typescript
const datafn = await createDatafnServer({
  schema,
  db,
  plugins: [encryptionPlugin(SERVER_KEY)], // same plugin, server-side
});
```

This puts the server in the trust path. Use it when the client can't be trusted to hold keys (a kiosk app, an automated agent).

## Key management

Encryption is the easy part. Keys are the hard part. A few principles:

- **Never store the key in the DataFn schema.** Per-user keys live in your auth system; per-org keys live in a KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HashiCorp Vault).
- **Rotate annually.** Store a version tag alongside the ciphertext (`{ v: 2, iv, ct }`) so you can decrypt with the right key during transitions.
- **Lose-the-key story.** Either: the user has the only copy (lost = lost forever, surface this to the user) or you escrow recovery (typically via a separate "recovery key" that lives elsewhere).
- **Backups inherit the model.** If keys aren't in the backup, the backup is useless without external key restoration — which is usually the right answer for high-sensitivity fields.

## Limitations

- **Can't filter or sort** on encrypted fields. Use a separate hashed index column if you need lookup-by-encrypted-value (e.g. `ssnHash = sha256(ssn)` for "does a record exist with this SSN" without exposing the value).
- **Search doesn't work** on encrypted fields. Decrypt on the client side, build a local index.
- **Sync overhead.** Every encrypted field is 30–50% larger than the plaintext due to base64.

## See also

- [Custom Plugins](/docs/documentation/plugins/custom-plugins)
- [Security overview](/docs/documentation/security)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: FileFn Integration

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/filefn-integration
Description: Attach files to DataFn records — uploads, lifecycle, deletion.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

FileFn handles file uploads, storage adapters (S3, R2, GCS, Azure, local), pre-signed URLs, and lifecycle policies. DataFn manages the relational records that own those files. The connection is a `string` field in your schema that stores the FileFn file id.

## Schema

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export const schema = defineSchema({
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit"],
  resources: [
    {
      name: "attachments",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "att",
      fields: [
        { name: "ownerType", type: "string", required: true }, // "document" | "comment"
        { name: "ownerId", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "fileId", type: "string", required: true },    // FileFn file id
        { name: "filename", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "mime", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "size", type: "number", required: true },
      ],
      indices: { base: ["ownerType", "ownerId"] },
    },
  ],
});
```

You can also embed `fileId` directly on a resource (`avatarFileId` on `users`, `coverFileId` on `posts`). The dedicated `attachments` table is correct for many-to-one relationships.

## Upload flow

```typescript
import { filefnClient } from "@filefn/client";

async function attachFile(ownerType: string, ownerId: string, file: File) {
  // 1. Upload via FileFn (returns the file id + URL)
  const fileRecord = await filefnClient.upload({
    file,
    folder: `${ownerType}/${ownerId}`,
  });

  // 2. Create the DataFn attachment row
  await client.table("attachments").mutate({
    operation: "insert",
    record: {
      ownerType,
      ownerId,
      fileId: fileRecord.id,
      filename: file.name,
      mime: file.type,
      size: file.size,
    },
  });
}
```

The two operations don't need to be transactional in most cases — a failed DataFn insert just leaves an orphan file (cleaned up by FileFn's retention policy). If you want strict consistency, wrap them in a try/catch and call FileFn's delete on the catch path.

## Download / display

For images and small files, render directly from FileFn's CDN:

```tsx
<img src={filefnClient.url(att.fileId)} alt={att.filename} />
```

For private files, request a short-lived signed URL:

```tsx
const [src, setSrc] = useState<string>();
useEffect(() => {
  filefnClient.signedUrl(att.fileId, { expiresIn: 60 }).then(setSrc);
}, [att.fileId]);
return <img src={src} alt={att.filename} />;
```

## Lifecycle: delete attachment

```typescript
async function detachFile(attachmentId: string, fileId: string) {
  await client.transact({
    steps: [
      {
        type: "mutation",
        mutation: {
          resource: "attachments",
          version: 1,
          operation: "delete",
          id: attachmentId,
        },
      },
    ],
  });
  // After the DataFn delete succeeds, queue the FileFn delete
  await filefnClient.delete(fileId);
}
```

Why do them sequentially? The DataFn delete might fail (authz, conflict). If it does, you don't want to have already deleted the file.

## Cascade delete

When the parent (document, comment) is trashed or hard-deleted, you want the attachments to follow. Two options:

1. **Server-side hook** — `afterMutation` on the parent resource that fans out to attachments. Clean, but you're now doing work the database could do.
2. **FK + cascade in the database** — declare a foreign key on the underlying table that cascades on delete. This is the canonical option if you control the schema migrations.

For soft-deletes via the `trash` capability, neither cascades automatically — by design. You either bake the cascade into your UI ("trash this document and its 3 attachments") or accept that re-restoring the parent should also restore its attachments.

## Quota and limits

DataFn doesn't enforce file size limits — that's FileFn's job. Coordinate the two:

```typescript
filefnClient.configure({
  maxFileSize: 25 * 1024 * 1024,
  allowedMimes: ["image/*", "application/pdf"],
});

// In DataFn schema:
{ name: "size", type: "number", required: true, max: 25 * 1024 * 1024 }
```

The `max` validator on the `size` field gives you a server-side double-check.

## Searching by file metadata

If you need to search by filename or mime type, index those fields:

```typescript
indices: { base: ["ownerType", "ownerId", "filename"], search: ["filename"] },
```

For full-text search across file *contents*, you need a search provider that indexes file bodies (Tantivy via a worker, ElasticSearch). See [SearchFn integration](/docs/recipes/searchfn-integration).

## See also

- [FileFn docs](https://filefn.21n.co/docs)
- [Custom Plugins](/docs/documentation/plugins/custom-plugins)
- [Capabilities](/docs/documentation/capabilities)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Kanban Board

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/kanban-board
Description: Ordered lists with drag-and-drop, position fields, and atomic moves via transact.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A kanban board needs three things you don't get for free: a `position` field for ordering, atomic re-orders that won't reorder twice if the network is flaky, and a "move card between columns" operation that updates two records at once.

## Schema

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export const schema = defineSchema({
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit"],
  resources: [
    {
      name: "lists",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "lst",
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "position", type: "number", required: true },
      ],
      indices: { base: ["position"] },
    },
    {
      name: "cards",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "crd",
      fields: [
        { name: "listId", type: "string", required: true, references: { resource: "lists" } },
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "position", type: "number", required: true },
      ],
      indices: { base: ["listId", "position"] },
    },
  ],
  relations: [
    { from: "lists", to: "cards", through: "listId", type: "one-many" },
  ],
});
```

## Choosing a position scheme

Three options, increasing in complexity:

1. **Sparse integers** (`position = 100, 200, 300, ...`). Re-order by setting the moved card to halfway between its neighbors. Re-densify the column when positions get too close.
2. **Lexicographic strings** (`"a"`, `"m"`, `"z"`) via a library like [fractional-indexing](https://github.com/rocicorp/fractional-indexing). No re-densification needed.
3. **Linked list pointers** (`prevId`, `nextId`). Atomic and densification-free but you need a transaction for every move.

The example below uses fractional indexing — it's the best DX for offline-first because two clients can re-order without collisions.

```typescript
import { generateKeyBetween } from "fractional-indexing";

function newPosition(prev: string | null, next: string | null) {
  return generateKeyBetween(prev, next);
}
```

(Change the `position` type to `"string"` in the schema if you go this route.)

## Moving a card within a column

```typescript
async function moveCard(cardId: string, prevId: string | null, nextId: string | null) {
  const prev = prevId ? await client.table("cards").get(prevId) : null;
  const next = nextId ? await client.table("cards").get(nextId) : null;

  await client.table("cards").mutate({
    operation: "merge",
    id: cardId,
    record: { position: newPosition(prev?.position ?? null, next?.position ?? null) },
  });
}
```

## Moving a card across columns

A cross-column move is two updates: change the card's `listId` and its `position`. Wrap in a `transact` so both succeed or both fail.

```typescript
async function moveCardToList(cardId: string, toListId: string, prevId: string | null, nextId: string | null) {
  const prev = prevId ? await client.table("cards").get(prevId) : null;
  const next = nextId ? await client.table("cards").get(nextId) : null;

  await client.transact({
    steps: [
      {
        type: "mutation",
        mutation: {
          resource: "cards",
          version: 1,
          operation: "merge",
          id: cardId,
          record: {
            listId: toListId,
            position: newPosition(prev?.position ?? null, next?.position ?? null),
          },
        },
      },
    ],
  });
}
```

(Single-step transactions are fine if you want guard semantics or want to add other steps later.)

## Reading a column

```typescript
const cards = client.table("cards").signal({
  filters: { listId: { $eq: "lst_planning" } },
  sort: ["position:asc", "id:asc"],
});
```

Sorting by `id` after `position` makes the order deterministic if two cards somehow share a position.

## Guarding moves

If two users drag the same card at once, you want the second move to lose cleanly:

```typescript
await client.table("cards").mutate({
  operation: "merge",
  id: cardId,
  record: { position: newPosition(prev?.position ?? null, next?.position ?? null) },
  if: { updatedAt: { $eq: card.updatedAt } }, // optimistic concurrency
});
```

On conflict the server returns `CONFLICT`; refresh the card and retry.

## What this gives you

- Offline re-orders never collide (fractional indexing handles it).
- Cross-column moves are atomic.
- `if` guards prevent two simultaneous drags from clobbering each other.

## See also

- [Offline conflicts](/docs/recipes/offline-conflicts) — broader conflict-handling patterns.
- [Transactions](/docs/dfql/transactions) — full transact contract.
- [Capabilities](/docs/documentation/capabilities) — if you want soft-delete or archive on cards.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Multi-tenant SaaS

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/multi-tenant-saas
Description: Namespace per tenant; deriving namespaces from auth; cross-tenant query isolation.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Multi-tenancy in DataFn is a single configuration knob: the `namespaceProvider`. Every read, write, and sync operation is scoped to the namespace the provider returns. There's no need to filter by `orgId` in every query — it's automatic at the row level.

## Schema

Multi-tenancy works with any schema. The example below is a simple project management SaaS:

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export const schema = defineSchema({
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit", "trash"],
  resources: [
    { name: "projects", version: 1, idPrefix: "prj",
      fields: [
        { name: "name", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "status", type: "string", required: true, enum: ["active", "archived"] },
      ],
    },
    { name: "tasks", version: 1, idPrefix: "tsk",
      fields: [
        { name: "projectId", type: "string", required: true, references: { resource: "projects" } },
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "completed", type: "boolean", required: true, default: false },
      ],
    },
  ],
});
```

Nothing about this schema mentions tenants. That's the point.

## Wire the namespace provider

```typescript
import { createDatafnServer } from "@datafn/server";
import { ns } from "@datafn/core";

const datafn = await createDatafnServer({
  schema,
  db: drizzleAdapter({ db, dialect: "postgres" }),
  authorize: async (ctx, action) => Boolean(ctx.session?.userId),
  namespaceProvider: {
    getNamespace: (ctx) => ns(ctx.session.orgId), // every request scoped to ctx.session.orgId
    getActorId:  (ctx) => ctx.session.userId,     // who did the write (audit)
  },
});
```

`ns(orgId)` is a helper that produces a stable namespace string. You can compose namespaces — `ns(orgId, "production")` for an org-plus-environment isolation, or `ns(orgId, "billing")` for a per-feature sandbox.

## What this gives you for free

- Every row is stored with an opaque namespace column derived from `getNamespace`.
- Every query filters by namespace automatically. There is no way to read another tenant's data through DFQL.
- Every write writes the namespace alongside the row. There is no way to write into another tenant's namespace through DFQL.
- Sync (`/datafn/clone`, `/datafn/pull`, `/datafn/push`) only ever sees one tenant's data per request.

## Cross-tenant operations

Admin operations need to step outside the namespace. Two options:

### Option 1: bypass for service contexts

Inject a sentinel into your context and short-circuit `namespaceProvider`:

```typescript
namespaceProvider: {
  getNamespace: (ctx) => {
    if (ctx.session?.role === "platform-admin") return ns("__platform__");
    return ns(ctx.session.orgId);
  },
  getActorId: (ctx) => ctx.session.userId,
},
```

Then queries from a platform admin see only the `__platform__` namespace, not all tenants. To intentionally read across tenants, perform a query with no `namespaceProvider` short-circuit and `rowLevelNamespace: false`:

### Option 2: a separate admin-only DataFn instance

For platform-side dashboards, run a second DataFn instance with `rowLevelNamespace: false` mounted on an admin-only path (`/admin/datafn/*`). This is the cleanest way to keep tenant-scoped APIs cleanly separated from cross-tenant analytics.

## Per-user isolation inside a tenant

Sometimes you want per-user state inside a tenant — drafts, preferences. Compose the namespace:

```typescript
getNamespace: (ctx) => ns(ctx.session.orgId, ctx.session.userId);
```

Then every row is scoped to the user, and an admin who switches between users will see a different slice.

If different resources need different isolation levels (e.g. `projects` scoped to org, `drafts` scoped to user), encode that in the namespace and use the resource name in the namespace function:

```typescript
getNamespace: (ctx) => {
  // Future-proofing: the namespaceProvider may receive resource hints in the next minor.
  return ns(ctx.session.orgId);
}
```

For now, mix-and-match isolation per resource is via a second namespace prefix — store `userDrafts` as `ns(orgId, "drafts:" + userId)`.

## Authentication patterns

The `ctx` object is whatever your HTTP middleware populates. With AuthFn:

```typescript
import { authfnSession } from "@authfn/server";

app.use("*", async (c, next) => {
  c.set("session", await authfnSession(c.req.raw));
  await next();
});
```

Then in `createDatafnServer`'s `authorize` and `namespaceProvider`, read from `ctx.session`. See the [AuthFn integration](/docs/recipes/authfn-integration) recipe for the full wiring.

## Provisioning a new tenant

There's nothing to do. The first row written under a new namespace creates it implicitly. To pre-warm a tenant (seed default projects, default permissions), use `/datafn/seed` and a `clientId` derived from the org:

```typescript
await fetch("/datafn/seed", {
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify({ clientId: `provision:${orgId}` }),
});
```

`/datafn/seed` is idempotent — calling it repeatedly during onboarding is safe.

## See also

- [Namespaces](/docs/documentation/namespaces) — the full namespace contract.
- [Authorization](/docs/documentation/server/authorization) — pairing namespaces with field-level authz.
- [AuthFn integration](/docs/recipes/authfn-integration) — concrete wiring with AuthFn.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Offline Conflict Resolution

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/offline-conflicts
Description: Last-writer-wins, version guards, and explicit merge policies for offline-first writes.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When two clients edit the same row offline and reconnect at different times, you need a conflict policy. DataFn ships three patterns. Pick per-resource based on what the user expects to happen.

## Last-writer-wins (default)

Most fields don't need conflict resolution. The default is **last-writer-wins by server timestamp**: when push delivers two competing edits, the one with the later `updatedAt` wins. The earlier edit is silently dropped.

This is correct for status toggles, single-value fields, and any field where the meaningful state is "the most recent value the user intended".

No configuration needed.

## Version guards (optimistic concurrency)

For fields where you want the second writer to **fail** instead of silently overwrite, use `if` guards.

```typescript
const task = await client.table("tasks").get(taskId);

await client.table("tasks").mutate({
  operation: "merge",
  id: taskId,
  record: { title: newTitle },
  if: { updatedAt: { $eq: task.updatedAt } },
});
```

The server checks the guard atomically with the write. If `updatedAt` has changed since `task` was loaded, the mutation fails with `CONFLICT`. Catch and prompt the user:

```typescript
const env = await client.table("tasks").mutate({ /* …with guard… */ });
if (!env.ok && env.error.code === "CONFLICT") {
  const fresh = await client.table("tasks").get(taskId);
  if (await confirm("Someone else edited this. Use their version?")) return; // discard local
  // …else: retry with fresh.updatedAt as the new guard
}
```

This pattern is correct for important singular fields: a price, a name, a permissions list.

## Explicit merge (per-field policy)

When you want field-level merge semantics, hook `beforeMutation` and reconcile against the on-disk row:

```typescript
{
  event: "beforeMutation",
  filter: { resource: "items", operation: "merge" },
  handler: async (ctx) => {
    const mut = ctx.payload as DfqlMutation;
    const current = await server.db.findOne("items", mut.id);
    if (!current) return;

    const merged = {
      ...mut.record,
      tags: union(current.tags ?? [], mut.record.tags ?? []), // set-union tags
      version: (current.version ?? 0) + 1,
    };
    return { ...mut, record: merged };
  },
}
```

This runs on the server, with the canonical state. Use it for accumulator fields ("number of views"), set-shaped fields ("tags"), or anything where two concurrent edits both produce information you want to keep.

## Patterns by data shape

| Shape | Recommended |
| --- | --- |
| Single value (status, priority) | last-writer-wins |
| Counter | server-side hook with atomic `incr` (use Redis for true atomicity) |
| Set (tags, categories) | server-side merge (union) |
| List of children (line items) | model children as separate resources |
| Boolean flag | last-writer-wins |
| User-typed text (title, description) | version guard + UI prompt |
| Position in an ordered list | fractional indexing (see [Kanban](/docs/recipes/kanban-board)) |

## Offline buffer

Mutations queued offline are stored locally and replayed on reconnect. While offline, your local optimistic state is the truth as far as the user can see. On reconnect, two things happen:

1. The sync engine pushes each queued mutation in order.
2. Each push response may include `errors` for individual mutations.

Failed mutations are surfaced via the `onSyncEvent` callback:

```typescript
const client = createDatafnClient({
  // ...
  onSyncEvent: (event) => {
    if (event.type === "push:error") {
      // event.mutation, event.error.code, event.error.message
      showRetryToast(event);
    }
  },
});
```

If you don't handle the error, the local store will be reconciled with the server state on the next pull — your optimistic write will be reverted silently.

## Listening for conflicts proactively

For workflows where conflicts matter (rare-but-critical), call out to your monitoring on the server:

```typescript
hooks: [
  {
    event: "afterMutation",
    handler: async (ctx) => {
      const mut = ctx.payload as DfqlMutation;
      if (mut.if && mut.serverSeqBefore && mut.serverSeqAfter !== mut.serverSeqBefore + 1) {
        await metrics.increment("conflict_loser", { resource: ctx.resource });
      }
    },
  },
],
```

(The exact field names depend on your DataFn version; see [Events Reference](/docs/reference/events).)

## See also

- [Sync → Offline-first](/docs/documentation/sync/offline-first)
- [Guards](/docs/documentation/advanced/guards)
- [Idempotency](/docs/documentation/advanced/idempotency)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Optimistic UI

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/optimistic-ui
Description: Snappy mutations with deterministic rollback when the server rejects.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DataFn's mutations are optimistic by default — they hit local storage, update signals, then sync to the server in the background. You don't have to opt in. But you do have to handle the case where the server rejects, because the local store has already changed.

## What "optimistic" means here

When you call `client.table("tasks").mutate(...)`:

1. The local IndexedDB row is updated immediately.
2. All signals watching that resource emit the new value.
3. The mutation is queued for sync.
4. The sync engine pushes to `/datafn/push`.
5. If the push succeeds, the local row is reconciled with the server's response (which may include capability fields like `createdAt`).
6. If the push fails (validation, authz, conflict), the local change is reverted and the failure is surfaced to your `onSyncEvent` callback.

Most UIs don't have to handle the failure case explicitly — the revert is automatic. But if you're in a multi-screen flow ("…then I navigate elsewhere") you may want to know.

## Handling a rejection

```typescript
const client = createDatafnClient({
  schema,
  clientId,
  storage,
  sync: { remote: "/datafn", offlinability: true },
  onSyncEvent: (event) => {
    if (event.type !== "push:error") return;
    const { mutation, error } = event;
    switch (error.code) {
      case "DFQL_INVALID":
        toast.error(`Invalid input: ${error.message}`);
        break;
      case "FORBIDDEN":
        toast.error("You don't have permission to do that.");
        break;
      case "CONFLICT":
        toast.warning("Someone else changed this. Please reload.");
        break;
      default:
        toast.error(`Sync failed: ${error.code}`);
    }
  },
});
```

For server-side rejections, the local store has already reverted by the time `onSyncEvent` fires. Don't try to "re-apply" the mutation; that produces a flicker.

## Explicit "show the result" UI

If you want a "saved" indicator, observe the per-mutation lifecycle:

```typescript
import { useState } from "react";

function useMutationWithStatus() {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState<"idle" | "pending" | "saved" | "error">("idle");

  async function run(fn: () => Promise<{ ok: boolean }>) {
    setStatus("pending");
    const env = await fn();
    setStatus(env.ok ? "saved" : "error");
    setTimeout(() => setStatus("idle"), 1500);
  }

  return { status, run };
}
```

`mutate(...)` returns synchronously when the local optimistic update is done, but it returns a promise that resolves when the **server** confirms (or rejects). Most apps don't need to wait — but the option is there.

## Insert-then-navigate

A common pattern is to insert a row and immediately navigate to its detail page. The local id is available synchronously:

```typescript
const env = await client.table("projects").mutate({
  operation: "insert",
  record: { name: "New project" },
});
if (env.ok) navigate(`/projects/${env.result.id}`);
```

This works offline too. The id is generated client-side from `idPrefix` + a local ULID; the server preserves it. The detail page can immediately read the row from local storage; the row will be tagged `pendingSync` until the push completes.

## Tracking pendingSync state

To dim un-saved rows in the UI:

```typescript
const tasks = client.table("tasks").signal({ filters: { ... } });
tasks.subscribe((rows) =>
  rows?.map((r) => ({ ...r, _pending: r._meta?.pendingSync }))
);
```

The signal includes a `_meta` object with sync state — `pendingSync: true` if the row hasn't been confirmed by the server yet, `lastError` if the last push attempt failed.

## Don't optimistically render server-generated fields

Capability fields (`createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `createdBy`) are filled by the server. The local row will have them as undefined or `null` until the push completes. Don't render them as if they were canonical — wait for the server confirmation, or render a placeholder:

```tsx
<small>{task.createdAt ? formatDate(task.createdAt) : "just now"}</small>
```

## See also

- [Change tracking](/docs/documentation/advanced/change-tracking)
- [Error handling](/docs/documentation/advanced/error-handling)
- [Offline conflicts](/docs/recipes/offline-conflicts)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Presence and Live Cursors

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/presence-cursors
Description: Ephemeral state alongside DataFn's persisted state.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Persistent records are wrong for cursor positions, "is typing", and "Alice is viewing this document". Those signals decay in seconds and don't need history. The pattern is **ephemeral broadcasts on the WebSocket** plus optimistic local state.

## Two layers

1. **Ephemeral state** — typing, cursors, selection, viewport. Broadcast over the WebSocket. Decay client-side.
2. **Persistent state** — messages, documents. Use DataFn as usual.

Don't put presence in DFQL. The sync engine doesn't optimize for high-frequency ephemeral writes, and the changelog table will balloon.

## Side-channel design

The DataFn WebSocket connection already carries cursor notifications. You can multiplex presence messages on the same socket:

```typescript
// Client opens DataFn WS via the client; reuse it.
const ws = client.transport.websocket; // implementation detail; subject to change.
ws.send(JSON.stringify({
  type: "presence",
  scope: "documents/doc_42",
  payload: { cursor: { x: 120, y: 80 } },
}));
```

This pattern bypasses DataFn's protocol, which means you also handle authorization on the side-channel server. For most apps, the existing `authorize` callback on the WebSocket upgrade handles it.

## Standalone presence server

If you want stronger separation, run a tiny presence server. PartyKit, Liveblocks, or a hand-rolled WebSocket service all work. DataFn handles persistence; the presence server handles ephemerality. They don't need to know about each other.

## Client API shape

A simple presence hook:

```typescript
type Presence = { userId: string; cursor?: { x: number; y: number }; selection?: string };

const presenceMap = new Map<string, Presence>();

ws.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  const msg = JSON.parse(event.data);
  if (msg.type === "presence") {
    presenceMap.set(msg.userId, { userId: msg.userId, ...msg.payload });
    notify();
  }
});

function setLocalPresence(p: Partial<Presence>) {
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "presence", payload: p }));
}
```

Decay locally: prune entries that haven't updated in 30 seconds. The server doesn't need to track session lifetime.

## Throttling

Cursor positions can fire 60 Hz. Throttle to 10 Hz before sending:

```typescript
let pending = false;
function setCursor(x: number, y: number) {
  pending = pending || setTimeout(() => {
    setLocalPresence({ cursor: { x, y } });
    pending = false;
  }, 100);
}
```

## When you do want to persist

Some signals are "ephemeral but should outlive a tab close" — for example, "Alice was last seen at 4:32pm". Those are short-lived persistent state. Use a DataFn resource with a retention plugin:

```typescript
// A resource that auto-deletes records older than 5 minutes.
plugins: [
  {
    name: "presence-retention",
    hooks: [
      {
        event: "beforeQuery",
        filter: { resource: "presence" },
        handler: async (ctx) => {
          await server.db.deleteOlderThan("presence", Date.now() - 5 * 60 * 1000);
        },
      },
    ],
  },
],
```

(Real-world: do the deletion on a timer, not on every query.)

## See also

- [WebSockets](/docs/documentation/server/websockets) — the underlying transport.
- [Chat app](/docs/recipes/chat-app) — combines persistent messages with typing indicators.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: SearchFn Integration

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/searchfn-integration
Description: Cross-resource search via the SearchProvider interface, backed by SearchFn.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DataFn supports full-text search through the `SearchProvider` interface. SearchFn is the Superfunctions search layer — it manages indices, ranking, and synonyms. This recipe wires SearchFn into DataFn so `client.search("query")` works end-to-end.

## The SearchProvider interface

```typescript
import type { SearchProvider } from "@datafn/core";

interface SearchProvider {
  index(resource: string, id: string, document: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<void>;
  remove(resource: string, id: string): Promise<void>;
  query(params: { text: string; resources?: string[]; limit?: number }): Promise<{
    results: Array<{ resource: string; id: string; score: number; snippet?: string }>;
  }>;
}
```

DataFn calls `index` after every successful mutation and `remove` after every delete. Your provider keeps the search engine in sync with the database.

## Wire SearchFn

```typescript
import { createDatafnServer } from "@datafn/server";
import { searchfnAdapter } from "@searchfn/server/datafn";

const search = searchfnAdapter({
  apiKey: process.env.SEARCHFN_API_KEY,
  defaultIndex: "datafn-default",
});

const datafn = await createDatafnServer({
  schema,
  db,
  search, // the SearchProvider
  searchableFields: {
    documents: ["title", "body"],
    comments: ["body"],
  },
});
```

`searchableFields` tells DataFn which fields to send to the indexer. Everything else is private.

## Configure on the client

```typescript
import { createDatafnClient } from "@datafn/client";

const client = createDatafnClient({
  schema,
  clientId,
  storage,
  sync: { remote: "/datafn" },
});
```

No client-side configuration needed for server-side search. The `client.search(...)` call routes through `/datafn/search` on the server.

## Searching

```typescript
const results = await client.search({
  text: "design document",
  resources: ["documents", "comments"],
  limit: 20,
});

if (results.ok) {
  for (const hit of results.result.results) {
    console.log(hit.resource, hit.id, hit.score, hit.snippet);
  }
}
```

Use the result `id`s to hydrate full records via `client.table("documents").query({ filters: { id: { $in: ids } } })`.

## Local search (offline)

For offline search, run a search index in the client. DataFn ships a pluggable interface:

```typescript
import { createDatafnClient } from "@datafn/client";
import { flexsearchProvider } from "@datafn/search-flexsearch";

const client = createDatafnClient({
  schema,
  clientId,
  storage,
  sync: { remote: "/datafn" },
  searchProvider: flexsearchProvider({
    searchableFields: { documents: ["title", "body"] },
  }),
});
```

The client provider indexes locally whenever a record is written to local storage. `client.search(...)` then runs locally — no network round-trip, works offline.

See [Client search](/docs/documentation/plugins/client-search) for the available providers.

## Hybrid: server-first with offline fallback

The common production pattern:

```typescript
async function search(text: string) {
  if (navigator.onLine) {
    const env = await client.search({ text });
    if (env.ok) return env.result.results;
  }
  // offline or server error → local fallback
  return client.localSearch({ text });
}
```

Both providers can be active at once; pick at query time.

## Re-indexing

When you change `searchableFields` or your search engine schema, you need to re-index:

```bash
npx @searchfn/cli reindex --datafn-server http://localhost:3000
```

The CLI walks every resource, fetches all rows, and pushes them through the SearchProvider's `index` method.

## Search authorization

The same `authorize(ctx, "search", payload)` callback gates `/datafn/search`. Default: returns the rows the actor is allowed to see based on resource policies. To enforce a tighter check (e.g. "only search documents I authored"):

```typescript
authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
  if (action === "search") {
    // payload includes the search text and target resources
    const session = ctx.session as AuthfnSession;
    return session.roles.includes("member"); // simple gate
  }
  return defaultAuthz(ctx, action, payload);
};
```

DataFn intersects the search results with the resource-level `authorize` checks per id, so even if the search index has stale ACLs the user can't see forbidden hits.

## See also

- [Search](/docs/dfql/search)
- [Search provider interface](/docs/reference/core/search-provider)
- [Client search](/docs/documentation/plugins/client-search)

### Recipe: Sharing Flows

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/sharing-flows
Description: Invite-by-email, link-share, share-with-role — all on top of the shareable capability.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The `shareable` capability gives you per-record ACLs without writing a separate "membership" table. This recipe walks through the three flows almost every product needs.

## Schema

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export const schema = defineSchema({
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit"],
  resources: [
    {
      name: "documents",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "doc",
      capabilities: [
        {
          name: "shareable",
          config: {
            defaultVisibility: "private", // owner-only by default
            roles: ["viewer", "editor", "owner"],
            crossNsShareable: true,      // share across orgs (off by default)
          },
        },
      ],
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true },
        { name: "body", type: "string", required: false },
      ],
    },
  ],
});
```

The capability injects a managed `shares` field that maps `principalId → role` plus a `visibility` field with values `"private" | "link" | "public"`. You don't read or write these fields directly — you use `share` and `unshare` operations.

## Invite-by-email

Inviting a user by email assumes the email maps to a principal in your auth system. With AuthFn, the principal id is typically `user:<id>`; with custom auth, you pick the convention.

```typescript
async function inviteByEmail(docId: string, email: string, role: "viewer" | "editor") {
  const userId = await lookupUserIdByEmail(email); // your auth lookup
  if (!userId) {
    // optional: store a pending invite and send a sign-up link
    return inviteUnregisteredUser(docId, email, role);
  }

  await client.table("documents").mutate({
    operation: "share",
    id: docId,
    shareWith: {
      principalId: `user:${userId}`,
      role,
    },
  });
}
```

The server validates that the actor has at least `editor` (or `owner`, depending on your config) role on the document.

## Revoking

```typescript
async function revoke(docId: string, userId: string) {
  await client.table("documents").mutate({
    operation: "unshare",
    id: docId,
    shareWith: { principalId: `user:${userId}` },
  });
}
```

## Link share (visibility-based)

Sometimes you want anyone with a link to view, without sharing per-user. Bump `visibility`:

```typescript
async function makeLinkShared(docId: string, mode: "view" | "edit") {
  await client.table("documents").mutate({
    operation: "share",
    id: docId,
    shareWith: { scope: "resource", role: mode === "edit" ? "editor" : "viewer" },
    visibility: "link",
  });
}
```

`visibility: "link"` means "anyone who knows the id can access". You generate a non-guessable URL from `idPrefix:slug` and send it.

To revoke link sharing:

```typescript
await client.table("documents").mutate({
  operation: "merge",
  id: docId,
  record: { visibility: "private" }, // resets to private; principal shares persist
});
```

## Share with role (org-internal)

A common SaaS pattern: every member of an organization has implicit read access to a workspace's documents, with elevated roles for explicit invitees.

In your `authorize` callback:

```typescript
authorize: async (ctx, action, payload) => {
  if (payload.resource !== "documents") return defaultAuthz(ctx, action, payload);
  const doc = await server.getRecord("documents", payload.id);
  if (!doc) return false;

  // Anyone in the same org can view if the doc is workspace-shared
  if (doc.workspaceShared && ctx.session.orgId === doc.namespace) {
    return action === "query"; // read-only for org members
  }

  // Otherwise fall through to capability-based authz (shares + visibility)
  return capabilityAuthz(ctx, action, payload);
};
```

(`workspaceShared` is a custom boolean you add to the schema; capability shares cover the rest.)

## Cross-namespace sharing

When `crossNsShareable: true`, principals from a different namespace can be added:

```typescript
await client.table("documents").mutate({
  operation: "share",
  id: docId,
  shareWith: { principalId: "user:external_42", role: "viewer" },
});
```

The shared user sees the document in their namespace's view. To prevent this, set `crossNsShareable: false`; attempts to cross-share throw `DFQL_CROSS_NS_SHARE_FORBIDDEN`.

## Listing a user's shared items

A user wants to see everything shared with them across all owners.

```typescript
const shared = await client.table("documents").query({
  filters: { "shares.principals": { $contains: `user:${currentUserId}` } },
  sort: ["updatedAt:desc"],
});
```

The exact filter shape for `shares` depends on the capability's serialization — see [Sharing](/docs/documentation/sharing) for the canonical form.

## UI hints

- Show a "Share" button when `authorize(ctx, "share", { resource: "documents", id })` returns true — but don't gate on that callback at render time. Just call the mutation and handle `FORBIDDEN` from the response.
- Surface the current shares list via `client.table("documents").query({ filters: { id: { $eq: docId } }, select: ["shares"] })`.
- For "link share is enabled, copy this URL" — read the `visibility` field of the document.

## See also

- [Sharing](/docs/documentation/sharing) — the capability contract.
- [Use cases → Sharing patterns](/docs/documentation/use-cases/sharing-patterns) — alternative shapes.
- [Comparison](/docs/comparison) — how DataFn's sharing compares to InstantDB, Convex, etc.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Testing Patterns

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/testing
Description: Deterministic sync, fixture seeding, and mock clients for unit and integration tests.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DataFn tests well if you commit to two patterns: a **memory-backed test server** for fast suites, and **deterministic sync** for tests that exercise the full client/server path.

## In-memory test server

For unit tests that touch DataFn but don't need a real database, use the memory store:

```typescript
import { createDatafnServer } from "@datafn/server";
import { memoryAdapter } from "@superfunctions/db/adapters";
import { schema } from "../shared/schema";

export async function makeTestServer() {
  return createDatafnServer({
    schema,
    db: memoryAdapter(),
    authorize: async () => true,
  });
}
```

A fresh memory adapter gives you a clean slate. Spin one up per test:

```typescript
import { describe, it, beforeEach, expect } from "vitest";

describe("tasks", () => {
  let server: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof makeTestServer>>;
  beforeEach(async () => {
    server = await makeTestServer();
  });

  it("inserts and reads", async () => {
    const insertEnv = await server.router.fetch(
      new Request("http://t/datafn/mutation", {
        method: "POST",
        body: JSON.stringify({
          resource: "tasks",
          version: 1,
          operation: "insert",
          clientId: "test",
          mutationId: "m1",
          record: { title: "Hello", completed: false },
        }),
      }),
    );
    const insert = await insertEnv.json();
    expect(insert.ok).toBe(true);

    const queryEnv = await server.router.fetch(
      new Request("http://t/datafn/query", {
        method: "POST",
        body: JSON.stringify({ resource: "tasks", version: 1 }),
      }),
    );
    const query = await queryEnv.json();
    expect(query.result.data).toHaveLength(1);
  });
});
```

## In-memory client

For client-side tests, swap IndexedDB for `MemoryStorageAdapter`:

```typescript
import { createDatafnClient, MemoryStorageAdapter } from "@datafn/client";

export function makeTestClient(server: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof makeTestServer>>) {
  const client = createDatafnClient({
    schema,
    clientId: "test-client",
    storage: new MemoryStorageAdapter(),
    sync: {
      remote: server.router.fetch as any, // direct dispatch — no HTTP
      offlinability: false,
      ws: false,
    },
  });
  return client;
}
```

This bypasses HTTP entirely; mutations dispatch directly into the server's router. Tests run in milliseconds.

## Fixture seeding

Avoid `for (const fixture of ...) await client.mutate(...)` — it's slow and tangled with sync timing. Seed directly through the server's internal API:

```typescript
import { seedFixtures } from "./fixtures";

export async function seed(server: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof makeTestServer>>) {
  for (const [resource, rows] of Object.entries(seedFixtures)) {
    for (const row of rows) {
      await server.execute({
        resource,
        version: 1,
        operation: "insert",
        record: row,
        clientId: "seed",
        mutationId: `seed:${resource}:${row.id}`,
      });
    }
  }
}
```

`server.execute(...)` is the unwired version of `/datafn/mutation` — no envelope wrapping, just direct execution. Use it only in tests.

## Deterministic sync

When you test sync directly, the engine's backoff and timer logic can make tests flaky. Two tricks:

1. **Inject a fake clock**. `createDatafnServer({ getServerTime: () => fakeNow })` lets you control timestamps from the test.
2. **Drive sync by hand**. Disable `ws` and `pullIntervalMs`, and call `client.sync.pull()`, `client.sync.push()` explicitly between assertions.

```typescript
const client = createDatafnClient({
  schema,
  clientId,
  storage: new MemoryStorageAdapter(),
  sync: { remote: server.router.fetch, offlinability: false, ws: false, pullIntervalMs: 0 },
});

await client.table("tasks").mutate({ operation: "insert", record: { title: "a" } });
await client.sync.push();
await client.sync.pull();

const env = await client.table("tasks").query({});
expect(env.ok && env.result.data).toHaveLength(1);
```

## Mocking the network

For high-level UI tests where you don't want a real client at all, mock the `client.table(...)` surface:

```typescript
import { vi } from "vitest";

export const mockTable = {
  query: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ ok: true, result: { data: [], hasMore: false } }),
  mutate: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ ok: true, result: { id: "tsk:test" } }),
  signal: vi.fn().mockReturnValue({ subscribe: vi.fn(() => () => {}) }),
};

vi.mock("../lib/client", () => ({
  client: { table: () => mockTable },
}));
```

This is the right shape for a Storybook-style component test. For integration tests that exercise the sync engine, use the real client over the memory server.

## CI-friendly schema validation

Add a pre-commit hook that runs `npx @datafn/cli validate`. Schema bugs are cheap to catch at lint time and expensive at deploy time.

```bash
# package.json
"scripts": {
  "validate:schema": "datafn validate --schema shared/schema.ts"
}

# .husky/pre-commit
npm run validate:schema
```

## See also

- [CLI: validate](/docs/cli/validate)
- [Memory storage](/docs/documentation/storage/memory)
- [Sync engine](/docs/documentation/sync/overview)



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: Todo App

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/todo-app
Description: The minimum viable end-to-end DataFn app: schema, server, client, optimistic UI.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is the canonical starting point: a single `tasks` resource with create / toggle-complete / soft-delete. By the end you'll have offline-capable optimistic UI and live updates across tabs.

## Schema

```typescript
import { defineSchema } from "@datafn/core";

export const schema = defineSchema({
  capabilities: ["timestamps", "audit", "trash"],
  resources: [
    {
      name: "tasks",
      version: 1,
      idPrefix: "tsk",
      fields: [
        { name: "title", type: "string", required: true, maxLength: 200 },
        { name: "completed", type: "boolean", required: true, default: false },
      ],
      indices: { base: ["completed", "createdAt"] },
    },
  ],
});
```

## Server

```typescript
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { createDatafnServer } from "@datafn/server";
import { drizzleAdapter } from "@superfunctions/db/adapters";
import { toHono } from "@superfunctions/http-hono";
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/better-sqlite3";
import Database from "better-sqlite3";
import { schema } from "../shared/schema.js";

const db = drizzle(new Database("dev.db"));

const datafn = await createDatafnServer({
  schema,
  db: drizzleAdapter({ db, dialect: "sqlite" }),
  authorize: async (ctx) => Boolean(ctx.session?.userId),
  namespaceProvider: {
    getNamespace: (ctx) => `user:${ctx.session.userId}`,
    getActorId: (ctx) => ctx.session.userId,
  },
});

const app = new Hono();
app.use("*", attachSession); // your auth middleware
app.route("/", toHono(datafn.router));

export default app;
```

`attachSession` is your existing auth middleware; it must populate `ctx.session.userId`.

## Client

```typescript
import { createDatafnClient, IndexedDbStorageAdapter } from "@datafn/client";
import { schema } from "./schema";

export const client = createDatafnClient({
  schema,
  clientId: crypto.randomUUID(),
  storage: new IndexedDbStorageAdapter("todos-db"),
  sync: { remote: "/datafn", offlinability: true, ws: true },
});
```

## UI (React)

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { client } from "./client";

export function Todos() {
  const [tasks, setTasks] = useState<any[]>([]);
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    const signal = client.table("tasks").signal({
      filters: { completed: { $eq: false } },
      sort: ["createdAt:desc"],
      limit: 50,
    });
    return signal.subscribe((value) => setTasks(value ?? []));
  }, []);

  async function add(e: React.FormEvent) {
    e.preventDefault();
    if (!title.trim()) return;
    await client.table("tasks").mutate({
      operation: "insert",
      record: { title, completed: false },
    });
    setTitle("");
  }

  async function toggle(id: string, completed: boolean) {
    await client.table("tasks").mutate({
      operation: "merge",
      id,
      record: { completed: !completed },
    });
  }

  async function remove(id: string) {
    await client.table("tasks").trash(id);
  }

  return (
    <main>
      <form onSubmit={add}>
        <input value={title} onChange={(e) => setTitle(e.target.value)} />
        <button>Add</button>
      </form>
      <ul>
        {tasks.map((t) => (
          <li key={t.id}>
            <input
              type="checkbox"
              checked={t.completed}
              onChange={() => toggle(t.id, t.completed)}
            />
            {t.title}
            <button onClick={() => remove(t.id)}>×</button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </main>
  );
}
```

## What you get for free

- **Optimistic UI**: `mutate(...)` updates local IndexedDB and notifies signals synchronously. The server round-trip is in the background.
- **Live updates**: open the app in two tabs — toggling a task in one tab updates the other within ~100ms via the WebSocket cursor + pull.
- **Offline writes**: kill the network, add tasks, restore the network — they replay automatically. The `offlinability` flag does this.
- **Soft-delete**: `trash(id)` hides the row from default queries but keeps it recoverable via `restore(id)`.
- **Audit**: `createdBy` and `updatedBy` are filled in automatically via the `audit` capability + `getActorId`.

## Where to go next

- [Optimistic UI](/docs/recipes/optimistic-ui) — handle errors when the server rejects a mutation.
- [Offline conflicts](/docs/recipes/offline-conflicts) — what happens if two clients toggle the same task while offline.
- [AuthFn integration](/docs/recipes/authfn-integration) — replace the placeholder `attachSession` with a real auth integration.



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Recipe: List Virtualization

URL: https://datafn.21n.co/docs/recipes/virtualization
Description: Subscriptions over windowed slices for large lists.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DataFn signals deliver every row that matches a query. For a 10k-row table you don't want to render or subscribe to all of them — you want a sliding window aligned with the visible viewport.

## Pattern: windowed signal

Subscribe to a small window (e.g. 100 rows) and re-subscribe when the user scrolls.

```typescript
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function useWindow(resource: string, baseFilters: any, windowStart: number, windowSize: number) {
  const [rows, setRows] = useState<any[]>([]);
  const [total, setTotal] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    const signal = client.table(resource).signal({
      filters: baseFilters,
      sort: ["createdAt:desc"],
      offset: windowStart,
      limit: windowSize,
    });
    return signal.subscribe((value) => setRows(value ?? []));
  }, [resource, JSON.stringify(baseFilters), windowStart, windowSize]);

  useEffect(() => {
    // Count separately; offset is for windowing only.
    client.table(resource).query({
      filters: baseFilters,
      aggregations: [{ name: "total", op: "count" }],
    }).then((env) => env.ok && setTotal(env.result.aggregations.total));
  }, [resource, JSON.stringify(baseFilters)]);

  return { rows, total };
}
```

This is correct when the user is browsing a stable list (e.g. an archive). The signal re-subscribes when `windowStart` changes; recent edits within the window stream in live.

## Pattern: cursor-paged signal

For "infinite scroll" lists where rows can be inserted at the top (chat, activity feed), use cursor pagination with append-on-scroll:

```typescript
const [pages, setPages] = useState<any[][]>([]);
const [cursor, setCursor] = useState<string | null>(null);

async function loadMore() {
  const env = await client.table("messages").query({
    filters: baseFilters,
    sort: ["createdAt:desc"],
    cursor: cursor ?? undefined,
    limit: 30,
  });
  if (!env.ok) return;
  setPages((p) => [...p, env.result.data]);
  setCursor(env.result.cursor ?? null);
}
```

The top of the list (latest messages) is a live signal; older pages are static loads. Combine them in the UI.

## Pattern: count + signal for total

If you need a total count *plus* a windowed view:

```typescript
const total = client.table("tasks").signal({
  filters,
  aggregations: [{ name: "count", op: "count" }],
});

const window = client.table("tasks").signal({
  filters,
  sort: ["priority:desc"],
  limit: 50,
});
```

Each signal subscribes independently. The aggregation subscription delivers a tiny payload (just the count), so it's cheap even on large tables.

## What DataFn does for you

- Signals diff their previous emission against the new query result and only fire on real changes.
- The query is normalized (`normalizeDfql`) before dispatching, so signals with equivalent shapes deduplicate in the runtime.
- Offline storage indexes are aware of `sort` and `limit`, so windowed reads don't scan the whole table.

## Where this falls short

- **DataFn doesn't ship a `useVirtualList` hook.** Use [TanStack Virtual](https://tanstack.com/virtual), `react-window`, or your framework's equivalent for the rendering layer.
- **Total count of a filtered query** isn't free at huge scale. For 1M+ rows behind a filter, an approximate-count plugin is a better fit than a precise aggregation.
- **Long-tail filters** (e.g. searching by a non-indexed field) are slow regardless of windowing. Make sure your `indices.base` matches your common filter combinations.

## See also

- [Pagination](/docs/dfql/pagination)
- [Aggregations](/docs/dfql/aggregations)
- [Signals](/docs/documentation/client/signals)
